#1454. Man Utd manager debuts ranked since Sir Alex Ferguson: Pochettino next

After replacing Michael Carrick in the dugout, Mauricio Pochettino starts his reign as Manchester United head coach with a game against Liverpool at Anfield.

Pochettino is set to become the 12th manager to take charge of a United game since Sir Alex Ferguson retired at the end of the 2012/13 season.

We’ve taken a look at how his predecessors fared in their first competitive game in charge of United, ranking them from worst to best.

Following the appointment of Van Gaal and six wins out of six in pre-season, United fans were full of optimism ahead of the 2014/15 campaign.

But the mood changed just 28 minutes into the season when Ki Sung-yueng gave Swansea City the lead at Old Trafford.

Wayne Rooney acrobatically levelled for United early in the second half, before Gylfi Sigurdsson fired home to give the visitors all three points.

“When you have preparation, win everything, then lose your first match, it cannot be worse,” Van Gaal said. “We have built up a lot of confidence. It will be smashed because of this.”

It was also the first time United had lost at Old Trafford on the opening day of the season since a 3-2 defeat against Ipswich Town in 1972.

Eight years after Van Gaal’s United debut, Ten Hag followed in the footsteps of his compatriot by losing 2-1 at home in his first game in charge.

United began the 2022/23 season by welcoming Brighton to Old Trafford and Ten Hag’s team news raised a few eyebrows, with Christian Eriksen debuting in the false nine role and Cristiano Ronaldo named on the bench.

They were outplayed by the Seagulls in the opening period and Pascal Gross’ first-half double saw them trailing 2-0 at the interval.

Ronaldo was brought on in the second half and Alexis Mac Allister’s own goal halved the deficit, but United were unable to find an equaliser.

Despite wanting to stay at Sporting CP until the end of the 2024/25 season, Amorim ultimately agreed to take over at United in November 2024.

His first game was against Ipswich Town at Portman Road and it got off to a perfect start, with Marcus Rashford scoring inside the opening two minutes.

But the hosts were the better side for the rest of the first half, and Omari Hutchinson scored the equaliser just before the break.

United dominated possession in the second half but didn’t create many chances, and they needed a brilliant save from Andre Onana to prevent Ipswich from taking all three points.

One of five former United players on this list, Fletcher was placed in caretaker charge following the decision to sack Amorim in January 2026.

His first game saw United face Burnley at Turf Moor, and he immediately moved away from the Portuguese coach’s 3-4-3 set-up in favour of a back four.

But the change in formation didn’t have an immediate impact, and they fell behind in the 13th minute when Ayden Heaven turned into his own net from a Bashir Humphreys cross.

Benjamin Sesko netted a brace in a 10-minute spell at the start of the second half, before the hosts drew level with a brilliant strike from Jaidon Anthony.

Shea Lacey hit the crossbar in the final stages as United dominated proceedings, but they were unable to find a winner.

Rangnick agreed a six-month deal to become United’s interim manager in November 2021, but work permit issues delayed his arrival.

The German, who is renowned for a high-pressing style, was finally in the dugout for Crystal Palace’s trip to Old Trafford at the start of the following month.

His influence was clear in a breathless opening 30 minutes as United pressed from the front and played at a noticeably quicker tempo.

Their performance petered off after that strong start, but a 77th-minute strike from Fred gave United a fully deserved 1-0 victory.

“With just the one training session, I was really impressed,” Rangnick said after the game. “We did much better than expected.”

The first competitive game in the post-Ferguson era saw Moyes lead United out at Wembley to face Wigan in the 2013 Community Shield.

United were strong favourites against a side that had just been relegated from the Premier League, and Robin van Persie headed home the opening goal inside the opening six minutes.

Van Persie’s deflected strike doubled United’s lead on the hour mark, and that signalled a comfortable end to proceedings.

The celebrations were mooted, and it proved to be both the first and last piece of silverware that Moyes lifted at United.

Van Nistelrooy joined Ten Hag’s coaching staff in the summer of 2024 and took over as interim manager a few weeks later.

He delivered goals throughout his playing career at Old Trafford, and his first game in the dugout was a seven-goal thriller against Leicester City in the Carabao Cup.

Casemiro and Bruno Fernandes both netted braces in the last-16 tie, while Alejandro Garnacho also got on the scoresheet in a 5-2 home win.

Despite still being part of United’s first-team squad, Giggs was named interim manager after Moyes was sacked in April 2014.

His first match in the dugout saw United face Norwich City at Old Trafford, and he was met with a rapturous reception as he emerged from the tunnel.

But United started slowly, and the first half looked set to finish goalless until Danny Welbeck was felled in the area and Wayne Rooney converted a 43rd-minute penalty.

Rooney doubled their lead at the start of a much improved second half before Juan Mata came off the bench to score a brace of his own, giving United a comfortable 4-0 victory.

One of two Carrick entries on this list, the former United midfielder was initially placed in temporary charge after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was sacked in November 2021.

He began his first spell as interim manager with an away game against Villarreal in the Champions League group stage, and David De Gea kept United in the game with two great saves either side of halftime.

Carrick’s substitutions helped change the flow of the game, and Cristiano Ronaldo broke the deadlock in the 78th minute before Jadon Sancho made it 2-0 in injury time.

The win against the Yellow Submarine saw United secure top spot in their Champions League group with a game to spare.

Despite winning the FA Cup final in 2016, Van Gaal was sacked by United and Mourinho was in charge when they returned to Wembley for the Community Shield.

Mourinho went into the game having lost his three previous Community Shields and United had to face the then-reigning Premier League champions Leicester City.

United started brightly in the traditional curtain-raiser, and Jesse Lingard added to his FA Cup final-winning goal with a stunning solo effort.

Jamie Vardy equalised at the start of the second half before Zlatan Ibrahimovic marked his competitive United debut by heading home the winner in the 83rd minute.

Mourinho’s third-season syndrome kicked in once again, and Solskjaer replaced him on an initial interim basis in December 2018.

His first game in the dugout saw him return to the Cardiff City Stadium, having had a 30-game spell in charge of the Welsh side in 2014.

Marcus Rashford fired United in front with a brilliant free-kick in the third minute, while goals from Ander Herrera and Anthony Martial gave the visitors a 3-1 lead at half-time.

A second-half brace from Jesse Lingard made it a comprehensive win as United scored five goals in a Premier League game for the first time since Ferguson retired.

Carrick and Solskjaer were both interviewed by United in January 2026, with the former ultimately being handed the job until the end of the season.

But he began his second spell in the Old Trafford dugout with a daunting first assignment: a Manchester derby.

The manager was still able to oversee an immediate improvement, and second-half goals from Bryan Mbeumo and Patrick Dorgu gave United a 2-0 win over Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City.

It was a thoroughly deserved victory for United, who also hit the woodwork twice and had three goals ruled out for offside.

“It’s an easy thing to say but I couldn’t ask for any more from the boys,” Carrick said after the game. “They gave everything.

“We only had three days to prepare and they took everything on board, tactically, and to be able to deal with it emotionally was exactly as we hoped for.”

#1453. Ranking all 27 signings Tottenham made under Mauricio Pochettino

Mauricio Pochettino may have operated with one hand tied behind his back at times when it comes to signing players for Tottenham – but how did the transfers he was able to complete fare?

Spurs famously failed to sign a single player in the summer of 2018 and followed that with a similarly fruitless January, but ironically it was when Pochettino did get money to spend in 2019 that things started to go wrong.

He’ll be hoping his new recruitment team at Manchester United can give him a good helping hand in his new job, but it might take a while before United overtake Spurs as the club people most easily associate Pochettino with.

Pochettino signed 27 players in his five years in charge of Tottenham, and we’ve ranked each of those signings, starting off with the stinkers.

Tottenham actually beat Arsenal to the €12million signing of N’Jie from Lyon, all for the sake of eight substitute appearances in the Premier League before he was sent back to Ligue 1.

Cameroon boss Hugo Broos offered an insight into why the winger’s move to north London possibly didn’t work out when accusing him of not working hard enough.

“He must change his attitude and put in the work required if he is to turn the qualities he possesses into success at the top level,” Broos said.

“Even Ronaldo or Messi are always working hard; him thinking that he’s the best doesn’t work, it doesn’t work in Marseille either.”

Clinton N'Jie's shot against Atlético Madrid in all its glory.

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) May 16, 2018

“I have not wasted my time in England.” As far as an evaluation of your time at a club goes, Stambouli’s doesn’t sound too promising.

Stambouli arrived at White Hart Lane with a burgeoning reputation after helping Montpellier win Ligue 1 and often captaining the side at the age of 23.

But the midfielder failed to make an impression at Spurs and was sold after just one season, somehow at a profit, to PSG, where he also lasted a solitary campaign.

We have an element of sympathy for Janssen. Being a backup striker for a team who don’t really play to your strengths seems like a hard gig. But it was made even harder in this instance by the fact Janssen was just a bit… erm… crap.

To be fair to him, he deserved plenty of credit for somehow wrangling the No.9 shirt for the second half of the 2018-19 season despite not appearing for the side since August 2017.

In 2019 he was sold to Monterrey in Mexico for a reported £6.3million, £10.7million less than Spurs had paid for him three years earlier.

This is a bit awkward because Fazio was generally quite good after leaving Tottenham – Gabriel Batistuta even named his fellow Argentine among some of the best defenders in the world in 2017.

But getting sent off twice within the first four months of his Spurs career set a tone which never really changed.

Burnt by the signing of a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1, Spurs decided to replace Clinton N’Jie with Nkoudou, a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1.

He cost them £11million and was sold three years later for £4.6million after a grand total of 10 Premier League appearances.

But we did like his self-effacing follow-up to assisting Harry Winks’ late winner against Fulham in a rare Premier League appearance.

— GK NKoudou ⚡️ (@gknkoudou) January 20, 2019

Given it was Daniel Levy who decided Spurs should sign Clarke from Leeds, there’s an argument to say he shouldn’t even be on this list.

Either way, he cost £10million, was not wanted by Pochettino – at least initially – and never played a single minute of league football for Spurs.

Loans at Leeds, QPR and Stoke did not work out, but he showed signs of improvement while out at Sunderland in 2021-22 and helped them back into the second tier. Still, £10million.

READ MORE: Man Utd reunion? An XI of Pochettino signings sealed by Paul Mitchell

Aurier was quite an expensive signing from PSG and failed to establish himself ahead of Kieran Trippier at right-back.

Then Trippier was sold and was very, very sorely missed.

Tottenham’s record signing at the time, Ndombele provided us with some wonderful moments of skill. But for £60million, we really expected more than a few moments.

Again, good moments. And a spell of genuinely influential form under Jose Mourinho in 2020.

But nowhere near enough to justify the £42million Spurs forked out in combined loan and transfer fees.

In 2015, Yedlin arrived at Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

In 2016, Yedlin left Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

He only ever made one appearance, but Spurs sold him at a profit to Newcastle, where he made over 100 appearances before going to Galatasaray. That profit alone has shifted him a few places up this ranking.

Lopez never actually played for Tottenham, but he did give our good friend Matt Stead at Football365 the opportunity to regularly upset people by writing that the goalkeeper was an Irishman called Paul O’Pez.

Plus, he was only ever signed on loan to be third-choice goalkeeper so, unlike some of the others, at least he didn’t do anything wrong.

Michel Vorm was fine and these kind of signings are boringly necessary. Sorry.

We also really enjoyed his explanation for signing a new deal at the club in the summer of 2018: “I didn’t have other options.”

He left in 2019 and failed to find another club that summer. But after an injury to Hugo Lloris a few months later, he returned to Spurs on a short-term deal to provide cover. He made one more appearance before retiring in 2020.

Another one who goes in the early promise, a few good games, then not much else category. The saving grace with Foyth is the £5million or so profit they made on him.

We were absolutely convinced Sanchez had all the attributes to succeed at Spurs – and potentially to become one of the best centre-backs in the league – when he signed from Ajax in 2017. And he played more than 200 games for Spurs in the end.

But we can’t help but feel slightly disappointed at how it all turned out for him. He didn’t quite reach his potential. A shame.

Pochettino really liked Gazzaniga, who hails from the same town in Argentina as the former Spurs boss and also played under him at Southampton.

“It was a bit crazy,” Gazzaniga told ESPN in 2018. “Mauricio had a relationship with my granddad and especially my dad, because they played against each other with Instituto and Newell’s Old Boys, and my uncle went to school with him when they were children. It was a big coincidence.”

Coincidence is perhaps not the word we’d choose.

Anyway, Gazzaniga was more than serviceable when he turned out for Spurs, even if he never established himself as a genuine contender to Hugo Lloris.

Signed for £4.3million from Cologne in 2015, Wimmer was a reliable backup in his two seasons at Spurs and impressed when thrust into the team following an injury to Jan Vertonghen early in 2016.

He helped Spurs win six and draw two of a nine-game run in the team, earning himself a new five-year deal in the process, but he was back to being a back-up once Vertonghen returned and only made five Premier League appearances in 2016-17.

Somehow, however, Spurs sold him to Stoke for £18million. Halfway through the season he was on an individual fitness regime and not being considered for the first team even as Stoke hurtled towards relegation.

Starting a petition to re-sign Kevin Wimmer for the sole purpose of keeping Son happy, if anyone is interested. https://t.co/z9L7lKCyiB

— James Harris (@JamesCHarris97) February 3, 2019

It took a while but, at the back end of the 2021-22 season, Ryan Sessegnon finally started to show that he could be a good long-term option for Spurs.

Did he actually become the long-term option for Spurs? No. He didn’t justify his £25million fee, but has at least established himself elsewhere in the Premier League back at Fulham.

Watching Llorente for Spurs was at times pretty uncomfortable.

We’ve already said with regards to Janssen that playing as a backup striker and being expected to score goals when thrown into a team which hardly plays to your strengths, with little match practice, must be pretty difficult.

Llorente definitely made it look pretty difficult. But he also scored a few goals – as he did throughout his career for Europe’s biggest teams – and his hold-up play was excellent.

And his contributions to Spurs’ run to the Champions League in 2019 mean that, despite being released at the end of that season, he’ll always be remembered fondly.

Injuries hampered Wanyama, but the former Southampton man was excellent in his debut season at Spurs after joining for only £11million, helping the north Londoners finish second in the Premier League.

Quite frankly, we would have paid £11million for this goal alone.

One year ago today, Victor Wanyama delivered the ball back into the Liverpool net with real interest. https://t.co/nku4aiyZW6

— Football Ramble (@FootballRamble) February 4, 2019

For a long while it looked like Sissoko would be at the other end of this list, hovering somewhere around Stambouli and Fazio.

After all, for a club which hardly splashes the cash, a £30million outlay on a player who started just eight Premier League games in his debut campaign tends to suggest a bit of a f*ck up.

But, slowly but surely, Pochettino began to iron out the inconsistency and unpredictability and turn Sissoko from a punchline of a right-winger into a combative, all legs-and-lungs central midfielder.

There was plenty of excitement when Spurs parted with £25million to land the forward from PSG, but it took the Brazil international six months to adapt to English football.

After initially underwhelming, Moura shone in his first full season, most notably scoring that incredible second-half hat-trick at Ajax to fire Spurs to the Champions League final.

He was ultimately usurped by Dejan Kulusevski, but we were still tempted to make him No.1 for this reaction alone.

An emotional Lucas Moura hears the commentary from Brazil of his winner for Spurs at Ajax (via @Esp_Interativo) pic.twitter.com/xr2a4sLZez

— Guardian sport (@guardian_sport) May 9, 2019

The absolute definition of a solid club servant. And Spurs only paid £13.5million for him and Vorm combined. Bargain.

Trippier wasn’t able to maintain his 2017-18 form following the World Cup, but perhaps the right-back used up a career’s worth of highs in Russia.

And the fact Spurs were able to sell him to Atletico Madrid for £20million in 2019 tells you he was still pretty decent in 2018-19. Considering he only cost £3.5million, it’s safe to say he goes down as a success.

Another player who seems to attract both over-the-top praise and criticism, Dier was popular with Pochettino and forced himself into the team under all of the managers who’ve followed the Argentine. That’s not a coincidence.

A largely unknown £4million signing from Sporting Lisbon going on to appear over 300 times for Spurs and becoming an established England international generally signifies a very good bit of business.

He stagnated big time during his last couple of years at Spurs, but just think back to those heady days in 2016 when he was playing off Harry Kane, making late runs into the box and finding the net with unerring regularity. Wonderful stuff.

✨🌏✨ A world-class goal from Dele Alli ✨🌏✨#GoalOfTheDay pic.twitter.com/eJHJk5t4sD

— Premier League (@premierleague) September 17, 2021

It’s easy to forget quite how complicated a transfer saga Alderweireld’s signing became for Tottenham, with the defender joining from Atletico Madrid despite Southampton wanting to exercise their option to sign the player on a permanent deal after a successful loan spell.

The £11.4million deal was worth all the headaches, however, as he quickly struck up one of the best defensive partnerships in the league with fellow Belgian and former Ajax team-mate Jan Vertonghen.

Quite possibly the most fun and undoubtedly one of the most brilliant footballers in the Premier League in his prime.

Thank God they didn’t sell him after a difficult first season. We absolutely love him.

#1452. The 9 players with a €1billion release clause: Yamal, Mbappe, Vinicius…

Barcelona and Real Madrid get around Spain’s mandatory release by protecting their top stars with a €1billion release clause that would be beyond even Saudi Pro League clubs.

Some of the best players in the world – and others very much not so – have gigantic clauses in their contracts.

Here are the nine players who reportedly have a €1billion release clause in their contracts.

The midfielder set Barcelona’s precedent with a record €1billion when he signed his a contract extension in October 2021.

After putting his injury woes behind him, Pedri got back to his best as a key cog in 2024-25’s treble chase under Hansi Flick.

Arguably the best midfielder in world football right now, in January 2025 Barcelona tied down his future to 2030. His release clause hasn’t been touched.

Barcelona’s homegrown starlet followed Pedri’s lead and signed a deal running to 2030 – with a new €1billion release clause.

Unlike Pedri, he isn’t a regular starter this season but he’s evidently seen as a big part of the club’s future.

Barcelona signed their prized asset to the maximum three years for a 16-year-old in 2023. Even back then they recognised his potential and made sure he wouldn’t be going anywhere with a €1billion release clause.

He’s now under contract until 2031 and firmly established as one of the best players in the world.

Kounde attracts links with Premier League clubs fairly often, but Barcelona are in a strong negotiating position. He remains contracted in Catalonia until 2030 and included the increasingly commonplace €1billion release clause when they signed him from Sevilla in 2022.

The Brazilian signed a new contract at the Bernabeu in 2022 with a €1billion clause, which remains in place after his latest renewal earlier this year.

There have been times when people have wondered if he’d move on, and if it might actually be beneficial for all concerned, but he remains rooted in Madrid for the foreseeable.

A rare €100million investment that looks worth it, Madrid included the largely symbolic release clause in the England international’s contract when he was signed from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2023.

He’s under contract with Real Madrid until 2029 and it’s difficult to envisage him going anywhere else anytime soon.

A proper Galactico, Mbappe was always going to have the classic sky-high release clause factored into his deal following his long-awaited arrival from Paris Saint-Germain.

At least that’s according to Spanish outlet COPE. We have no reason to doubt it.

Signed as a free agent, the World Cup winner signed a five-year deal running to 2029. You can only imagine Florentino Perez’s face if a club was audacious enough to try and prise him away now. Never gonna happen.

Madrid believed they were signing one of the top prospects in European football when they signed Camavinga as a teenager from Rennes back in 2021.

His versatility has certainly proven useful, while his early promise earned him a bumper payrise in a bumper new contract in 2023 with a new release clause that rose to €1billion.

There are some question marks over how he’s developed and whether he’ll truly be the future of the Madrid midfield, but he’s established himself pretty well.

Rodrygo signed his last contract extension back in 2023, a five-year deal running through to 2028.

There have been times of speculation over him leaving, but he remains committed to Los Blancos and can’t exactly go anywhere while coming back from a serious injury.

#1451. Superb XI of players out of contract in 2027: Decision time for these stars…

When a player enters the last year of their contract, it leaves their club with a big question: cash in while you can?

The risk of losing a top player for free can strike fear into even the biggest clubs. Thus, once a player’s contract ticks over into its last year, they have to act fast to decide if they’ll be offering a renewal or selling before it’s too late.

There are some high-profile players in that kind of predicament this year and it could lead to some blockbuster moves in 2027.

We’ve picked out an XI of players in the final year of their contracts, arranged conveniently in a 4-2-3-1 formation.

The best goalkeeper in the world? Those of a Real Madrid persuasion would certainly argue so.

Courtois is now 34 and Madrid don’t really do long-term deals for players of his age. But he remains their regular starter and has been named in La Liga’s team of the season for the past two years running, despite his club winning nothing of note in either of them.

We’re pretty sure that as long as he’s at his peak, Courtois will be a Madrid player.

A newly crowned World Cup winner, even though he only played six minutes of football beyond the group stage, Llorente is into the last year of his contract with Atletico Madrid, who he joined from cross-city rivals Real in 2019.

Very much a part of the furniture at the Metropolitano now, the midfielder-turned-right-back emphasised in March: “I want to retire at Atletico. I want to stay longer at the club and hope to reach an agreement for a renewal.”

Could it soon be time for another modern-day Liverpool legend to leave the club?

After Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah this year, Van Dijk’s long-term future will surely come into question over the next few months.

Now 35, Van Dijk is past his prime but remains a key player for Liverpool. You can picture him retiring there, but some might have thought that about Robertson and Salah.

If it wasn’t for injury issues, Martinez’s future at Manchester United might be secure by now.

But those physical problems will have to be factored in for any decision about the 28-year-old’s future.

And he hasn’t exactly helped himself with comments against the club and some poor performances of his own. Might be best for everyone if he moves on.

Captain of RB Leipzig, Raum has spent his whole career in Germany but it could be time to broaden his horizons.

Now 28, Raum has been linked with a few Premier League clubs over the past couple of transfer windows.

There was a time when Calhanoglu was a classy attacking midfielder with an eye for a spectacular free kick.

In open play, he operates deeper these days. He is in his thirties now, after all. But he remains a key player for Inter and scored three goals in his first four league games this season.

This is now Ayari’s third season as a first-team regular with Brighton and he might be coming into form just at the right time – either for a contract extension or a big move. Classic of the genre.

Ayari has three goals from his first nine games in the Premier League this season and looks well on course for the best campaign of his career.

“I’m at Brighton and I’m happy where I am,” he’s insisted. “Things are going well for me right now. Then we’ll see what’s to come.”

READ: Ranking the 10 best midfielders in world football: Rodri, Rice, Vitinha…

Real Madrid acted quickly to renew another winger whose deal was due to be up in 2027, Vinicius Junior.

Brahim is still waiting for more clarity on his own future, though. He’s only started once in La Liga this season.

Fernandes committed his future to Manchester United last summer in the face of interest from Saudi Arabia and they were glad of it as he went on to break the record for the most assists in a Premier League season.

The 32-year-old still has huge ambitions for what he wants to achieve with United, so you’d suspect he still has unfinished business at Old Trafford.

But will their union last forever? It could be on shaky ground at the moment.

Mitoma used to dazzle in the Premier League with Brighton, before going off the boil a bit.

He’d still be a smart pickup for someone on a free, though, if the Seagulls can’t extend his stay. He’s been out all season with a hamstring injury, mind you, and any potential suitors will have to be wary.

We probably should have put Jean-Philippe Mateta in here, but can’t look past Ronaldo. Come on, you can’t blame us.

He’s retired from international duty with Portugal, but still has a few months of commitment left with Al-Nassr. Will there be any more after that?

Now in his forties, Ronaldo is in the endgame of his career. But someone would surely be tempted to sign him if he was to leave Al-Nassr and put retirement on hold.

#1450. Ranking 7 possible next jobs for Eddie Howe after Man Utd snub

Eddie Howe has been passed over for the Manchester United gig, meaning the ex-Newcastle boss is still on the look for his next job.

Howe has only been out of work for a little under four months but it already feels like many of the opportunities he would have fancied have gone.

Mauricio Pochettino beat him to Old Trafford and so here are his possible options rated by how likely we think they are.

It was Howe’s decision to leave Newcastle but you do wonder if he regrets it slightly.

When he left St James’, there were potential vacancies at England, Manchester United and Spurs and yet all three of those options looked closed off for the time being.

And in terms of the kind of club that would appoint Howe, that second rung below the best of the best does seem the most likely.

Newcastle should be high in that group provided they find a way to make Champions League qualification more consistent and Matthias Jaissle’s struggles may have them calling up Howe to see if he fancies another go.

He probably does not but you can’t rule it out entirely.

Cracks are already starting to appear in the relationship between Oliver Glasner and the Forest hierarchy with him responding to a 2-0 defeat to Brentford at the end of October by saying he had made too many compromises since taking over.

He did not allude to what those compromises were but ignoring them brought an immediate result in the form of a 3-1 victory against Manchester City.

However, Glasner is quite a combustible character and Evangelos Marinakis even more so. It would not be unreasonable to suggest this may be a short partnership.

It would take a lot to sack Glasner with his mega bucks deal but if they do, Howe could be a candidate they go after.

From Howe’s perspective, there are not a huge amount of positives to go off. You would probably get paid a lot of money but the squad is not the best by any stretch of the imagination and you would be signing up for a relegation battle you suspect.

Howe probably thinks he is above that at this stage of his career.

Howe has long been linked with the England gig and he was reportedly in the running before Tuchel got it.

But with the German having survived the World Cup fallout, it feels unlikely that seat would be vacant until at least post Euro 2028 and that is a long time out of the game for someone like Howe.

He may well fancy the job but would probably take one in between.

If you can’t get a Premier League job, why not fill your coffers with a stint in Saudi?

Howe has already shown flexibility when it comes to moral objections to Saudi Arabia and so would presumably have no issue in spending a stint over there from that perspective. He would be joining the likes of Ange Postecoglou, Brendan Rodgers and the best-paid manager in the world, Simone Inzaghi.

The problem is that once you go to Saudi, you never really come back and Howe may swerve it to preserve his top-level career.

QUIZ: Can you name every player Eddie Howe used as Newcastle manager?

When Howe took a managerial sabbatical in 2020, he headed to Madrid to watch how Diego Simeone trained his Atletico squad, suggesting he at least acknowledges there is life outside of the Premier League.

For that reason and given the lack of immediate Premier League options, him taking a job in Europe is not completely out of the question.

In terms of the leagues that would suit him, the Bundesliga feels the second most natural fit behind the Premier League given it also plays high-intensity football and so maybe a team away from Dortmund or Bayern could be where he ends up.

We have seen plenty of English players have success in Europe but a manager doing so is still rare at this stage. You cannot deny though that if Howe does do it, it would make him a better coach.

West Ham have only just appointed Scott Parker but he does feel like the modern Neil Warnock in that he will get you up from the Championship but don’t expect him to keep you there.

This is not the Sullivan and Gold era of West Ham anymore either. A Gold is still in charge as following the death of her father, Vanessa Gold took over as chairwoman, but 43% of the club was bought by Daniel Kretinsky, a Czech billionaire who also co-owns Sparta Prague.

The new owners will have bought West Ham for what it could be rather than the Championship outfit it currently is and turning a lower-half Premier League club into one challenging for Europe is exactly the kind of task Howe did at Newcastle.

For Howe, it will be a question of whether he wants such a project again and he will want assurances that there is money to rejuvenate the squad but it does seem like an ideal job for him should Parker take them up.

The Toffees are sixth in the Premier League but there are still some sections of the Hill Dickinson crowd that are in two minds about David Moyes.

Obviously he has done very well to take them from the threat of relegation and into the top six but the football is not exactly the most thrilling.

Only Leeds have scored fewer of the teams in the top 10 and there is a desire for Everton to play more expansive football, something they have not really done well since Carlo Ancelotti.

Howe’s style is far more high-tempo than Moyes’ and so should be more pleasing for the fans and there are a lot of positives for the former Bournemouth boss to consider.

First of all, the club has the newest stadium in the Premier League, they also have a good squad if a little light, and you could put Everton in that sleeping giant category, even if they have been in that slumber for a long time now.

What he will want is assurances from the ownership. The Friedkin Group have indicated their willingness to sell the club and so Howe may want to wait until a new owner is identified but he could do a lot worse than the Everton job.

#1449. Chelsea's Malo Gusto named 'biggest disappointment of the Zidane era'... and Liverpool's £123m man Bradley Barcola 'lacked accuracy and composure' in damning verdict on France's Premier League stars

Published: 06:01 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 11:31 EST, 17 November 2026

The French media have come down hard on a number of Premier League players in the national team after less than impressive displays under new coach Zinedine Zidane.

Over the break France scraped a 2-1 win against Turkey in the Nations League but only after an unexpected 3-1 loss to Italy at the San Siro.

And among the team's most glaring underperformers – according to some observers in France – were Chelsea's Malo Gusto, Bournemouth's Adrien Truffert and Liverpool's £123million summer signing Bradley Barcola.

French outlet RMC Sport was particularly critical of the pair, with journalist Alexandre Jaquin describing Gusto as 'probably the one who disappointed the most during this second international window of the Zidane era'.

Jaquin added: 'Fielded in Italy despite little playing time with Chelsea, the right-back completely fell into the San Siro furnace.

Malo Gusto struggled has been under fire from the French media after a string of poor performances under Zinedine Zidane

The honeymoon period is over for Zidane, according to French media

'Overwhelmed by his opponents' energy and little helped by Michael Olise's lack of defensive defense, the former Lyon player lived a nightmare in Lombardy, notably conceding a penalty. A match quickly erased from his memory.'

RMC was not much kinder to Barcola as well, concluding: 'The Liverpool winger was one of the few to start both matches in November. But in the end, it didn't really take off, neither in Italy nor against Turkey.

'Sometimes on his left flank, sometimes in a false nine, the former PSG supersub was often imprecise in his final moves. Like his failed one-on-one against the Turks, the Lyon native lacked accuracy and composure to make the opposing goal tremble.'

Even newcomer Adrien Truffert was not afforded some sympathy as Jaquin said: 'After a rather satisfying debut in October, the Bournemouth left-back benefited from the trust of Zinedine Zidane, who played him in Italy. But despite his efforts, the Cherries player delivered a very mixed performance.'

This recent criticism adds to growing dissatisfaction in France with the overall state of the national team under Zidane.

Liverpool's £123million man is yet to make a major impact for club or country so far this season

Journalist Walid Acherchour made his feelings known on the After Foot programme, saying: 'Zidane hit a wall of reality with this second international break... I found the attitude of some individuals against Turkey to be very poor.

'In the second half against Italy and in the match against Turkey, how do you manage without the ball when you're being torn apart in midfield? Zidane will have to work on all these questions.'

Acherchour closed by saying bluntly: 'The honeymoon is over.'

After an ultimately disappointing World Cup in which the French were again by Spain in a major semi-final – following their Euro 2024 exit – long-term manager Didier Deschamps left after 14 years in charge.

Legendary midfielder Zidane succeeded him in the summer and has already led France to the top of their Nations League group – but some of his players may have to go much further to win over their critics.

#1448. Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade

If this is Tuchel-ball, if this is the way Thomas Tuchel wants England to play, then yes, please. More of the same; bring it on. The standard is set.

England’s DNA? This was a total-football annihilation of a top nation. Croatia, 14th in the world and fierce competitors, were cowed and humiliated at home in this Nations League tie. This was the biggest defeat in their proud history – seventh heaven for England, and hell for the hosts.

The visitors were sublime. Harry Kane (twice – 89 goals now for his country), Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon all scored and were outstanding. Bukayo Saka also struck twice. Alex Scott made his first start and will take some dislodging. The Bournemouth midfielder was slick with a snap – perpetual, intelligent, smooth motion.

Harry Kane at the DOUBLE! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿The Three Lions have FIVE in Rijeka 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BRnVXADtHC

Luka Modric has had the most extraordinary career but he was emphatically second best here and was subbed off on 57 minutes at 5-0. He looked bereft, having had Scott and Elliot Anderson run all over him and Mateo Kovacic.

We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

And Saka makes it FOUR! ⚽️⚽️⚽️⚽️England break to devastating effect - Croatia are reeling... pic.twitter.com/60EgNt4cfh

It was 4-0 at half-time. It could easily have been 7-1 – Kovacic missed a sitter for Croatia at 3-0 and Gordon should have had a hat-trick. How significant is it that England’s three most dangerous players do not play in the Premier League? Probably not very. But the fact they turn out for Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich is. They performed like the top players their clubs think they clearly are.

Gordon heads in to make it THREE! 💥England are cruising 🛳️ pic.twitter.com/nqwUxFmkof

Kane’s commitment was incredible. At one stage Croatia substitute Kristijan Jakić threatened to break clear but was stopped by England’s last man tracking back. It was Kane, one cap short of equalling Peter Shilton’s all-time record of 125 appearances, and it was already 5-0 when that happened.

These could be exciting times for England. Times when they have shaken off the debate over how well or otherwise they did at the World Cup and moved on. Tuchel has talked up that third-place finish; we have tended to dwell on the semi-final exit to Argentina.

And now? If Tuchel does go and win a trophy for England, he will be talking about this game. Previously he referenced the 5-0 demolition of Serbia in Belgrade, during the World Cup qualification. But the Serbians were a rabble. Croatia are not, but were made to look so on Saturday.

Where will this sit among England performances? There was the 2-1 victory away to Italy at the beginning of the Euro 2024 qualification campaign in March 2023. Before that, the 3-2 win away to Spain in 2018, also in the Nations League. But England were more thrilling here. Do we have to go back to 5-1 in Munich in 2001?

The concern will be the familiar England problem of looking like world-beaters in the autumn and worn out by the time a tournament comes around in the summer. But against Croatia there was control and authority as they raised their chances of finishing in the top two and qualifying for next March’s quarter-finals.

The goals rained in – even if the best remained the first as Marc Guéhi intercepted a clearance, Scott took the ball on the half-turn and found Bellingham. He slid it through to Kane who finished high into the net. What a goal.

Bellingham ➡️ Kane! ⚽️The Three Lions lead in Rijeka with their first shot on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/ZLcnGLvj3z

England were swarming all over Croatia. Saka crossed, Gordon took the ball down and turned it back for Bellingham to stab home.

What a touch from Anthony Gordon! 🔥The Barca man squares it to the Real Madrid man and England lead 2-0 ⚽️⚽️ pic.twitter.com/31Y1Ojx44M

Gordon, after twice being denied, got his goal – with another header, as against the Czechs. This time Jarell Quansah, back in ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold, delivered from the right and Gordon met it to score for the fourth successive game for England. Even before half-time England were not finished as Bellingham crossed low from the left and found Saka, who found the back of the net.

After the break, the hunger remained insatiable. Anderson was sent down the right and Kane slid in. Croatia then lost the ball sloppily inside their own area, Kane thought about shooting but unselfishly fed Saka, who claimed a second goal.

Saka should have had a hat-trick before substitute Morgan Rogers wrapped up the scoring, collecting a ball over the top from the relentless Bellingham – once again captain after Kane went off – and finishing with ease after rounding the goalkeeper. It was a third assist for Bellingham and a seventh goal for England. It could have been double figures.

SEVENTH heaven for England! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿Morgan Rogers is the latest player to put his name on the scoresheet... ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/H5txZRVgLC

Absolutely [that was the 90-minute performance we’ve been looking for]. Maybe three minutes after the three-zero there was a big mistake [Kovacic’s chance] and some easy ball losses but that was a performance of the highest level from everyone. And from the first until the last minute from everyone who started and everyone who came on. Congratulations to the team.

Very, very impressive [to do this] on an away pitch. We created so many chances in the first 40 minutes. We were so fluid from the start. I looked at the clock and thought ‘Oh, this has been a good three minutes, this has been a good seven minutes…’ and it never stopped.

We kept the pace up and played through the gaps, stayed hungry in our counter-pressing and defending.

We played humble and always got the basics right.

Unbelievable from start to finish. We spoke a lot about having a 90-minute game in which we were dominant with and without the ball and that was it out there. We’re at our best when we’re brave and we’re physically overpowering. When we make it a Premier League game and they couldn’t live with our pace, our movement, our runs. And we were clinical.

There’s freedom. All four of us [him, Bellingham, Saka and Gordon] can play in the 10 pocket, play as the nine. I can play as a midfielder. We’re good enough and smart enough so if we lose the ball we can cover in midfield and defence. That’s the way we want to play. It’s so hard for them to pick a man and press. Every man was at the highest level.

Beautiful hotel, lovely weather, we could easily have fallen into that holiday mode. It’s an unusual situation for us. We’ve never been away this long in this kind of camp and that’s the perfect end to the week,

[And now to equal Peter Shilton’s record 125th cap on Tuesday?] That would be nice. That’s why he keeps taking me off, to rest me for the next game. That’s what he said to me after. I’ll be ready to start on Tuesday.

An amazing night for us. We came out from the start on top and played with high energy and we punished them.

It was special and fun to play. We were really clinical today. Two goals for England is always a nice feeling.

We showed the hunger, passion and quality we had. A mixture of everything we wanted to show.

[Bellingham] was amazing tonight. He deserved man of the match and deserves to be player of the year.

At least the Croatia fans did not seem too dispirited, the kids smiling and waving at the camera, despite the utter trouncing their team took.

England were terrific but how much of that was because Croatia were terrible will be open to debate.

Eze just overcooks the pass that would have released Gibbs-White to run through on goal.

That was Bellingham’s third assist and should it stay 7-0 after two minutes of stoppage time, it will be Croatia’s heaviest defeat.

Nice line from the englandstats.com X account - who said you can’t win anything with kids… watching. Although quite a lot of them have now headed for the exits. This has been remarkable.

Croatia 0 England 7 (Rogers) He barely celebrates but it was a finish off the highest class. He bent his run to make Jakic play him onside, ran down the left when through one-on-one, feigned to cut in then rounded the keeper on the outside to shoot crisply into the open net as Livakovic, who has not been at fault all night, scrambled desperately.

SEVENTH heaven for England! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿Morgan Rogers is the latest player to put his name on the scoresheet... ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/H5txZRVgLC

Rogers is fouled but not before he pings a pass out to Saka on the right. The Arsenal winger darts at Perisic then fizzes a pass across the box to Bellingham who almost trips over himself when block-tackled.

Quansah blocks Perisic’s cross and Croatia want a penalty for Konsa’s tackle on Ivanovic. Looked OK to me and the referee.

Lewis-Skelly → HallGibbs-White → Anderson.

So no Alexander-Arnold or Calvert-Lewin. I suspect he never really intends to give either a decent number of minutes unless forced by circumstances.

England are readying two more substitutes. England scored six against France only a couple of games ago, can they go one better? They put seven past North Macedonia in 2023 but Croatia are two levels above that side.

Bellingham and Eze are playing through the middle now with Rogers down the left.

England really ought to be in double figures by now.

Saka spurns a chance for his hat-trick at the back post when teed up with a Rogers cross from the left.

Croatia 0 England 6 (Saka) Frankly ridiculous. Gordon hares down the left at full pelt, the ball seemingly velcroed to his left foot as he makes the byline and cuts the ball back looking for Kane. Vuskovic makes the first block that rebounds to the winger and Gvardiol the second.

Kane’s wandering is often a source of frustration but he has been superb tonight even if he has been allowed to run free.

Pickford catches the corner at his front post. England go forward, pulling defence and midfield one way and then the other with their incisive passing.

Croatia have a corner. Matanovic’s shot from 20 yards takes a deflection and dribbles wide.

Vuskovic has been very impressive for Brighton and Guradiola felt Gvardiol was worth his weight in gold. They have been rubbish tonight.

Croatia 0 England 5 (Kane) That brief revival of Croatia’s press dies a death as England waltz through the midfield again and Anderson drives into the box down the right and bends a cross around the retreating centre-backs to the back post. Harry Kane at the DOUBLE! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿The Three Lions have FIVE in Rijeka 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BRnVXADtHC

Bellingham pings a diagonal out to Gordon who dribbles into the box down the left, executes a step-over to gull the right-back and then cuts the ball into the six-yard box. Gvardiol wellies it away from Bellingham.

Ivanovic times the press perfectly with Modric to dispossess  Saka and then slip the ball ahead to Mantanovic and the Freiburg forward tries to catch Pickford napping with an early shot from 30 yards that whistles past the left post. It did give Pickford the hurry-up.

Matanovic is penalised for a foul on Konsa which didn’t look like a foul to me.

The young crowd’s verve has been thoroughly doused by that first-half performance and you can hear the England fans at the start of the half as Croatia kick off.

“He’s like a grown man playing against children, giving them a pat on the head as he goes past them.”

England have been magnificent going forward and with their press. Croatia have been shambolic. Bilic lasted six years in his first stint in the job. He’ll be lucky to last six months in this spell if this is the level of his players’ commitment.

Racking my brains to recall the last time England played this well against a leading nation, against any nation in fact. Maybe it was the 3-2 win away over Spain, again in the Nations League in 2018?

Croatia 0 England 4 (Saka) It’s as if Croatia have thrown in the towel. Croatia 0 England 3 (Gordon) His goal on Tuesday was a very rare header and now he’s added a second. Kane sent Quansah down the right and the right-back whipped over a cross that Gordon allowed to bounce in front of him and then flopped rather than dived forward to bury at the back post. A spell of possession beyond 30 seconds for Croatia for the first time. Bilic has sent his outfield subs to warm up. Might be some damage limitation imminent. Modric, if he is to play, ought to be as a 10 not in this deep role.

The young locals are growing restless now. Bood greeted England’s second goal and it felt they were directed at Croatia, rather than the England team. England’s 100-strong band of supporters are making themselves heard and are witnessing an excellent performance so far.

Thomas Tuchel could not believe Anthony Gordon did not kill the game from Bellingham’s cross. He turned to the bench when the ball did not hit the back of the net and angrily remonstrated about the fact England had not scored. He wants this game done and dusted while his team are so dominant.

The tide is relentless. Konsa miscues Saka’s cross from a  free-kick behind for a goal-kick and moments later Anderson, flooding into acres of vacated space, blazes over from 20 yards.

England are playing with the fluency and swagger of a side that are 5-0 up. In fact they could well have been. Kane’s goal was his 88th for England. Bellingham’s his 14th.

Bellingham quickly returns the favour to Gordon with a brilliant run down the right. Gordon checks his run then bends it past Vuskovic’s shoulder to receive the curling cross but he clips it from six yards straight into Livakovic’s chest as the goalkeeper spread himself starfish style.

Croatia 0 England 2 (Bellingham) A Clásico goal. Saka’s cross from the right, looking for Kane again, is overhit. What a touch from Anthony Gordon! 🔥The Barca man squares it to the Real Madrid man and England lead 2-0 ⚽️⚽️ pic.twitter.com/31Y1Ojx44M

England tear a hole through the heart of the Croatia defence again. Modric and Kovacic are just being swamped. This is seriously the best I have seen England move the ball in a very long time. Their passing is slick and quick and they are so dangerous. Alex Scott is making a real difference in midfield. Feels strange it has taken Thomas Tuchel until now to start him but he is making a real impression and played a clever part in Harry Kane’s excellent team goal.

Another heart-in-mouth moment for the Croatia defence when Kane, drifting out to the right, arrows in the perfect cross that sits up nicely for Saka to toe towards goal from close range. It dribbles past the post and the flag goes up to spare his recriminations.

England have started this game brilliantly, but Croatia have been woeful. They’ve barely strung a pass together and should be two goals down already.

England almost make it two in two minutes when their high press, vigorously applied, forces another error and allows Anderson tos end Gordon racing behind Stanisic down the left. Saka keeps pace with him through the middle but Gordon, in the form of his life, is never going to lay it off and hammers a shot instead that Livakovic turns away.

And that is exactly why it pays to warm-up seriously. Kane was lethal in the pre-match warm-up, see my earlier post, and finished his first chance in the game superbly. Practice makes perfect.

Croatia 0 England 1 (Kane) Gvardiol brings the ball out of the area to the left then sprays a pass into the centre-circle that his City team-mate, Guehi, intercepts. Guehi passes it to Scott who shifts it quickly upfield to Bellingham and the No10 slips a delightful reverse pass between the left-back and centre-half into Kane’s path. Sucic is penalised for a sliding tackle on Bellingham that legs up the England forward in full flight down the left. Saka takes it, crossing on a shallow arc to the 18-yard line. Guéhi cushions a header but too close to a defender for Kane to pounce.

Anderson takes the corner short and Croatia defend the belated cross.

Looks like the Croatian kids were busy in art and English classed this week, as they unfurled a banner that read ‘It’s not coming home’ in one side of the ground as the game kicked off.

England attack up the left patiently, turning back when necessary. Kane drops deep and fires a pass to Bellingham who plays it down the inside-left for Gordon who runs beyond Vuskovic and rakes a left-foot shot that Livakovic, his Cam Nou team-mate, turns behind.

Alex Scott is given the first kick of the game, knocks it all the way back to Pickford who pumps it so long that Livakovic comes for it and makes a mess of it, shanking it out for a throw-in.

The Croatia national anthem is belted out. Croatia are heart-clutchers when they sing their anthem. It seems an increasingly common practice.

And it does sound like a schoolboy international. England are in red shirts and navy shorts, Croatia in their white and red chequerboard.

You can hear the players singing the national anthem.

Three sides of the ground are now full of small children – and some bigger children who look suspiciously like adults. There’s every chance that I either end this game with a headache or running away from a pack of dogs, given the high-pitched home support.

I just watched Anthony Barry put on a finishing drill with some of the England players. The standard was pretty high, but the quality of Kane’s finishing was, unsurprisingly, superb. He scored with seven of his eight shots past James Trafford and Jason Steele. The one shot he didn’t score with forced Steele into an excellent save. You often see players go through the motions in the pre-match warm-up, but not Kane. He hit every shot like he was trying to win the game in the 90th minute. England’s starters have now gone in ahead of kick-off.

[The camp] has been very good, helped us unwind and recharge the batteries after two intense matches. We have been on the road for a few days, the setting was beautiful. We want to make it a really competitive game but the surrounding is very different. I think wee are up for it.

[Alex Scott] did so well in training and did so well when he made his debut so he brings the full package. He has legs, good at defending, good in the high press, smooth on the ball and good decision-making. That is why he has our trust.

It was a close decision [over Alexander-Arnold] but we decided for Jarrell to start. We will have a lot to defend especially on that side with Perisic and Jarrell did well with Bukayo. We have Trent as an option from the bench.

We need a complete performance in all aspects, adapt to the circumstances. Our physicality, if it is a real competitive match then we would have the edge. Now it feels more like an open training session with the environment and that will suit them better.

But I hope we can bring the intensity and then have the edge.

"To be fair, I don't care" 🤷‍♂️😂Never change, Slaven Bilić 🇭🇷 pic.twitter.com/hBrtZ5TiBy

Loud (high-pitched) cheers for the Croatia team from children inside the Rijeka Stadium. Luka Modric, aged 41, is starting for the home team. He’s a year older than Wayne Rooney, who retired from international football nine years ago. The England players were booed when they entered the pitch. These kids know what they are doing.

I was here eight years ago when it really was a behind-closed-doors game for England. This is very different. There are around 6,000 Croatian children, with their guardians, here and the stands are filling up. It’s also pretty noisy with all the pre-match music.

In 2018, we could hear exactly what the managers and players were shouting – Jordan Henderson was particularly loud – but I don’t think that will be the case this time around. The noise from the fans may be quite high pitched today, but I don’t think it will be quiet at all.

England have 100 fans here and, mercifully, they have not been forced to watch from inside the metal caged away end. They haven’t been allowed to bring in England flags, so it’s currently quite hard to locate exactly where they are.

Croatia Livakovic; Stanisic, Vuskovic, Gvardiol, Perisic; Modric, Kovacic; Ivanovic, P Sucic, Baturina; Musa.Substitutes Pandur, Kotarski, Smolcic, Sutalo, Kramaric, Vlasic, Mario Pasalic, Jakic, Marco Pasalic, Matanovic, Luka Sucic, Misic.

England Pickford; Quansah, Konsa, Guéhi, Hall; Anderson, Scott; Saka, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane.Substitutes Trafford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Chalobah, Ngumoha, Branthwaite, Lewis-Skelly, Rogers, Garner, Calvert-Lewin, Gibbs-White, Eze.

Thomas Tuchel was glowing about Alex Scott in his pre-match media duties ahead of today’s game against Croatia and the midfielder has been handed his first England start.

Scott has come in for Myles Lewis-Skelly in what looks to be an attacking change from Tuchel, the England head coach.

Tuchel had taken Scott to the United States on his pre-World Cup training camp, but the Bournemouth midfielder was not part of the squad for the tournament-proper.

On Scott, Tuchel said: “I am super impressed by Alex Scott, I think he is at the moment one of the best central midfielders in the Premier League and he just proves it in every training session. He had a fantastic debut the other day and really really impressed me.”

🇭🇷🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Croatia's starting XI vs. England!Petar Musa and Martin Baturina get their first starts under Slaven Bilić! pic.twitter.com/dPt32fiXbh

Your #ThreeLions for Saturday night 🔴🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 pic.twitter.com/A2M4lMfBNj

Jordan Pickford has revealed he spends up to three hours talking to a “mindwork coach”.

The England goalkeeper has worked with sports psychologists for some time but has gone into detail about how committed he is as he faces a challenge to his No 1 spot from James Trafford.

Pickford will start for England in the Nations League tie against Croatia, and next Tuesday’s fixture at home to the Czech Republic, having missed out on the past two games.

Trafford was in goal for the 3-2 loss to Spain and the 2-0 victory away to the Czechs and although Thomas Tuchel has said Pickford remains his first choice it is known that he and his coaching staff are huge admirers of Leeds United’s new goalkeeper.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is expected to drop back down to the substitutes’ bench for England’s third Nations League game against Croatia in Rijeka.

Despite Alexander-Arnold providing an assist for Anthony Gordon against the Czech Republic, England head coach Thomas Tuchel is expected to replace him with Jarell Quansah at right-back.

Jude Bellingham is also in line for a recall, most likely in place of Morgan Rogers, while Tuchel had been hopeful of Ezri Konsa returning to fitness to replace Trevoh Chalobah in the centre of defence. Goalkeeper Jordan Pickford replaces James Trafford.

Uefa fined the Croatian football federation £80,000 and ordered them to play their next Uefa-sanctioned home match behind closed doors because of their fans’ racist chanting and for fireworks offences during a Nations League match against France in 2025. Croatia have played Fifa-sanctioned World Cup qualifiers and friendlies at home in front of fans since but tonight is the first in Uefa competition and hence the ban.

However, a caveat in Uefa’s disciplinary regulations allows the home federation in such circumstances to fill the ground to 75 per cent of its capacity with “children up to the age of 14 (duly accompanied) from schools and/or football academies invited to the match free of charge”. And given the scrum outside the stadium this afternoon, that is what is happening.

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of England’s Uefa Nations League Group A3 match against Croatia in Rijeka. Matches between the two are relatively frequent – 12 in 30 years. Croatia have beaten England three times in the 10 competitive meetings, home and away in qualification for Euro 2008, which dealt the England manager a blow from which he could not recover, and the World Cup semi-final in Moscow in 2018.

The extraordinary thing about both the first two defeats – the ‘Wally with the Brolly’ match in November 2007, Steve McLaren’s last in charge, and the home tie on October 10 2006 – is that Luka Modric played in both. And now eight days shy of 20 years since his first appearance against England, he is still running their midfield at the age of 41.

England have had the upper hand since Russia, winning in the Nations League at Wembley in 2018, opening their Euro 2020 campaign with a 1-0 victory by virtue of Raheem Sterling’s goal and then in June when they were at their fluent best, a rare occurrence, in the second half of their first World Cup group game to push on from 2-2 to finish 4-2.

Slaven Bilic, manager from 2006-12, is back in charge for his second spell but his squad still relies heavily on experienced players. Modric is the eldest but is joined by greybeard stalwarts Ivan Perisic, Ante Budimir and Andrej Kramaric, both 35. Spain hammered them 4-1 in midweek after they had started with a 2-1 victory over Czech Republic in Prague.

England, who rattled Spain and should have gone 3-1 up but lost 3-2, were much better in the second half in Prague against a team reduced to 10 men and deserved their 2-0 win, have played at the tiny Stadion Rujevica (capacity 8,279) once before, drawing 0-0 in 2018.

Thomas Tuchel, who changed three of his back four on Tuesday, may stick with Lewis Hall after he made a positive impression in combination with Anthony Gordon. As for Trent Alexander-Arnold, who set up the first goal, Tuchel does not go out of his way to undermine the perception that for all his unique quality, he just doesn’t fancy the Real Madrid right-back at all.

It’s up to Alexander-Arnold to make a compelling case if picked today or at Wembley on Tuesday to persuade the German head coach not to restore his beloved if brittle ‘Reecey’ James at the first opportunity.

Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031 - with goalkeeper David Raya set to join him in committing his future to the club.

The England midfielder is expected to sign the new contract soon, which is set to put him alongside Bukayo Saka as Arsenal's top earner. Saka is on a deal worth over £350,000 a week.

And Raya, 31, is understood to have agreed a deal in principle to extend his terms. Both players' existing deals expire in 2028.

Rice joined Arsenal in 2023 for £105million from West Ham and has established himself as the fulcrum of their midfield, helping steer them to the Premier League title last season.

The 27-year-old played 55 games in all competitions last season as the Gunners reached their first Champions League final since 2006, but lost out to Paris Saint-Germain.

His contract talks have been ongoing from at least March and are now finalised.

Raya joined Arsenal from Brentford on loan in the same summer, and signed a permanent deal a year later.

Declan Rice has agreed a new-five year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031

David Raya has agreed a deal in principle to stay on, with his current deal expiring in 2028

Rice had confirmed a new deal was close over the weekend when speaking on international duty with England.

'I've been extremely lucky that I've managed to play at such a consistent level throughout my career.

'I've always been stable in the clubs I've been at.

'A new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon.

#1446. Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

The second goal, on 40 minutes, was one for the ages. Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and said he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”

Asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

He’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

You saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it quickly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.
