All panels are based on MaxQuant data analysis and, where applicable, use peptide intensities.

Four of the five teeth, PA1796, PA1799, NX-B1-127 and NX-B2-9, contain peptides uniquely matching to amelogenin-Y, a protein transcribed and translated from AMELY, a gene located on the hominin Y chromosome (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 2). These teeth therefore derive from genetically male individuals36,37,38. Conversely, for the fifth tooth, NX-A1-123, no such peptides were identified in any of the three search strategies, despite overall similar protein preservation in this tooth. We therefore identify this specimen as a genetic female. Together, this indicates that endogenous peptides were preserved in and identified from five hominin teeth, four males and one female, from Naxian and Baxian caves.

Our palaeoproteomic data analysis strategy used PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant in parallel. Sequence coverage and protein identification were highly consistent among all search strategies used (Supplementary Notes 3 and 4). PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant sequence reconstructions agreed in all recovered amino acid positions except for one, which was subsequently excluded from the generated consensus sequences for each specimen. In total, between 566 and 1,440 (including collagen type I), or between 556 and 808 (excluding collagen type I), amino acid positions could be reconstructed (Extended Data Table 2 (tab 1)). In an Asian context, this sequence coverage is comparable to the dental enamel proteomes recovered from the Middle Pleistocene Denisovan Penghu mandible (695 positions)7, the Middle Pleistocene Denisovan from Tam Ngu Hao 2 (558 positions)6, the Denisovan Harbin dental enamel proteome (903 positions), the Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from Zhoukoudian and Sunjiadong (440–599 positions)13 and the range of amino acid positions recovered from Pleistocene Pongo from East and Southeast Asia32,33, but above the number of positions reconstructed for an Early Pleistocene Gigantopithecus specimen from southern China30 and two Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from Hexian13. Among the consensus sequences generated for each hominin tooth, we find no positions uniquely derived in the genus Pongo, conclusively rejecting an attribution of these teeth to the orangutan lineage (Table 1).

Protein sequence variation among Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans is known to be low for dental enamel proteins29,39,40. For the protein regions reconstructed here, in our reference database, the single available Denisovan reference proteome has two uniquely derived substitutions (AMBN M273V and COL1A2 R996K; Table 1). For AMBN M273V, all five individuals from Naxian and Baxian caves carry the ancestral methionine, while the single individual with coverage for COL1A2 R996K, PA1799, also has the ancestral arginine for this position. No other amino acid positions uniquely derived in Early Pleistocene hominins, Neanderthals or modern humans are covered by the data obtained from the studied fossil specimens.

Our analytical strategy revealed the presence of a single amino acid polymorphism at position 253 of ameloblastin (AMBN, UniProt:Q9NP70), where an alanine is replaced by a glycine. The substitution was independently picked up in initial PEAKS analysis for Naxian and Baxian caves, and subsequently confirmed by MaxQuant and pFind analysis (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Four out of five studied hominin teeth (NX-A1-123, NX-B1-127, NX-B2-9 and PA1799) carry peptides uniquely matching the derived version of the sequence, AMBN(A253G), which probably results from a Cys to Gly transition in the codon GCC to GGC (chromosome 4: 70603880–70603882). The peptides matching this novel derived substitution do not match to known bacterial or fungal sequences. The substitution is not present in the available reference genomes or proteomes for Neanderthals (Vindija 33.19 (ref. 41), Chagyrskaya (ref. 42), Denisova 5 (ref. 43)) or the Denisovan high-coverage genome (Denisova 3)44. The ancestral alanine is also the amino acid previously reported for the dental enamel proteomes from the Penghu 1 and TNH2-1 Denisovans6,7. The substitution is absent in the great ape reference proteomes available to us45, nor is it present in the human gnomAD exome database (v.4.1, 1,461,678 individuals) or the 1000 Genomes and SGDP datasets45,46,47. The substitution was not observed in the H. erectus proteome published for D4163, a specimen dated to approximately 1.77 Ma from Dmanisi, Georgia, which contains the ancestral alanine29. However, the derived glycine was observed in six H. erectus teeth dating to approximately 0.4 Ma from East Asia. The AMBN A253G substitution therefore appears to be widespread among East Asian H. erectus13. Although the derived AMBN A253G substitution is so far exclusively observed among East Asian H. erectus specimens, this does not exclude the possibility that other specimens belonging to this population carried the ancestral amino acid variant.

In this tree, Denisova 3 is the only included Denisovan individual, while ZKD, SJD14M, HX-S1, HX-S2, SJD10A and SJD10M refer to H. erectus specimens studied previously. b, Amino acid occupancy for reference great ape specimens, including extinct and extant hominins, for three selected dental enamel protein positions relevant for the five Naxian and Baxian hominin specimens studied proteomically in this study. c, Selected peptide-spectrum matches showing coverage of the H. erectus-derived AMBN-253G substitution observed in four of the Naxian and Baxian hominins. Peptide fragment ion series extracted from PEAKS Online v.12.

Although individual variation in protein amino acid sequences can exist between individuals, we find, among the regions of the proteins covered in our ancient data, only a single position with sequence variation among the worldwide distributed modern humans included in our database search (Table 1). In general, among extant hominids, out of the 43 amino acid positions variable among and between great ape individuals included, and in cases in which we have coverage for at least one of the four hominins studied here, only five positions contain sequence heterogeneity between the included individuals where at least four or more individuals of a single genus share variation (one position in H. sapiens, three in the genus Pan and one in the genus Pongo; Table 1). Notably, the four teeth carrying the derived AMBN A253G substitution shared with the previously reported H. erectus specimens from Zhoukoudian, Sunjiadon and Hexian differ from those six specimens, as the Naxian and Baxian hominins do not carry the derived AMBN M273V substitution (Table 1, Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Thus, the observation of the AMBN Gly253 substitution combined with the observation at AMBN Met273 in four hominin teeth, of at least three individuals, if the two M1s from Naxian cave represent the same individual, from two late Middle Pleistocene sites suggests that the hominin population to which they collectively belonged has not previously been sampled using molecular methods, either genetic or proteomic.

To further explore the phylogenetic placement of the Naxian and Baxian specimens, we conducted a Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. Note that, owing to the sparseness of dental enamel proteomic data, such analyses in palaeoproteomics generally have to assume that there has been no recent gene flow between the individuals and populations included in the analysis. We find that the four Naxian and Baxian individuals with the AMBN A253G substitution cluster together in a clade outside the branch of previously reported Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The topology of the clade formed by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans matches the expected configuration in the main analysis, albeit with low internal node support (Fig. 4). The topology of these three hominin populations changes once additional modern human and great ape individuals are added to the phylogenetic analysis (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The expected topology of this clade is challenging to obtain when using proteomic data from dental enamel proteins, as reported previously29,39,40, and it is evidenced by the low support value of this clade in our analyses (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6). Nevertheless, the values supporting the nodes for the remaining branches, including the one placing the Naxian and Baxian specimens as an outgroup to the other hominins, are high in all analyses (>0.995). The Naxian and Baxian individuals are placed in a clade together with six previously reported H. erectus specimens. Those six specimens are placed together with strong support and separate from the four Naxian and Baxian individuals carrying the AMBN A253G substitution (Fig. 4). This strengthens the notion that these four Naxian and Baxian cave specimens represent a H. erectus hominin population that has not been sampled molecularly before. Furthermore, the phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans. These phylogenetic observations are in accordance with the morphological analysis of these specimens, strengthening the case that these specimens belong to a previously unsampled lineage of H. erectus.

By contrast, proteomic analysis of PA1796 from Baxian cave reveals that this specimen does not contain the derived AMBN A253G amino acid substitution (Extended Data Fig. 6b). It has no uniquely derived substitutions compared to the other four teeth, nor does it share uniquely derived amino acid substitutions with the Denisovan, Neanderthal or modern human individuals present in our reference panel (Table 1). Phylogenetic analysis of this specimen places it outside of the H. erectus clade, with varying topologies with low support in relation to its placement in relation to archaic hominins (Denisovans and Neanderthals) or the clade including Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 6a). The protein sequences reconstructed for this tooth are therefore different from the other four specimens studied proteomically, mirroring the morphological analysis that also indicates this specimen represents a taxon other than H. erectus. Only a single Denisovan genomic reference is currently available, the D3 specimen from Denisova cave, Russia, implying that our understanding of protein sequence polymorphisms for Denisovans is by definition limited. Future morphological and genomic or proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region could provide additional frameworks to allow more precise taxonomic classification of PA1796 into a non-erectus group, representing either southern Asian representatives of Denisovans (H. longi) or potentially another population or species.

Eight of the late Middle Pleistocene Homo teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves exhibit metric and morphological features that lie within the range of East and Southeast Asian H. erectus and that differ from those of Denisovans (H. longi), Neanderthals (H. neanderthalensis), or Pleistocene and Holocene modern humans (H. sapiens). The palaeoproteomic evidence provides further confirmation that four of these teeth indeed fall outside of the known genetic and proteomic sequence variation of H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens, but are consistent with a H. erectus-derived substitution recently described for Chinese specimens dating to around 0.4 Ma (ref. 13). The recovered proteomic evidence is therefore compatible with the morphological data. Dated to between 324 and 184 ka (ref. 12), these H. erectus teeth substantially extend the known temporal range of H. erectus fossils on the Asian mainland, bringing the extent of the mainland H. erectus fossil record closer to the latest known Javanese H. erectus, dated to 117–108 ka (ref. 8). The recovery of a unique proteomic signature of mainland H. erectus from the Middle Pleistocene of East Asia furthermore suggests that specimens attributed to this species could harbour several hominin populations13, and make it possible to molecularly test whether other H. erectus fossils from the region that could potentially date to the late Middle Pleistocene, such as those from Changyang cave (Hubei province, China)11,22 and Chaoxian cave (Anhui Province, China)23, also represent specimens belonging to the same mainland H. erectus hominin population, or whether they have a proteomic signature more similar to earlier H. erectus13.

The discovery of the Naxian and Baxian H. erectus specimens in the late Middle Pleistocene of southern East Asia enriches the hominin occupation scenario in the region. A Denisovan mandible has been described from the Penghu channel off the coast of Taiwan, dating to either 190–130 or 70–10 ka (refs. 7,48). In Laos, based on morphological analysis, a Denisovan molar has been described from Tam Ngu Hao 2, dating to between 163 and 131 ka (ref. 6). Genetic evidence on the timing of Denisovan introgression into the genomes of living humans also suggests that Denisovans were present in East and/or Southeast Asia well into the Late Pleistocene1,49. Moreover, several craniodental remains, such as Harbin, Penghu 1 and Xiahe 1, were identified molecularly as H. longi (Denisovans)7,9,17,19, and several other late Middle Pleistocene specimens probably belong to this population as well (for example, Xujiayao and Hualongdong), including also some non-erectus fossils from southern Asia (for example, Maba, Narmada, TNH2-1)6,50. It therefore seems plausible that the H. erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins.

Even though the geometric morphometric analysis of the EDJ suggest that the PA1796 M2 retains plesiomorphic aspects (mostly due to the short EDJ height), the specimen also differs from the morphology of the comparative H. erectus sample (Supplementary Note 2). The lack of a comparative sample for Denisovans (H. longi) represents a substantial bias in our ability to morphologically identify them. The non-metric morphology of PA1796 differs markedly from that of Chinese H. erectus by the lack of wrinkling on the EDJ, the absence of accessory fossae, the relatively large talon and the lingually shifted hypocone25,26 (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). Moreover, the palaeoproteomic analysis of PA1796 shows a different signal compared to the other Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as to the six H. erectus teeth from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong13 (Fig. 4), strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than H. erectus in Baxian cave. However, among the protein sequences available to us now, the PA1796 specimen does not exhibit the known proteomic variation associated with Denisovans, although it should be acknowledged that only a single Denisovan reference genome is currently available. PA1796 could therefore either represent a still-unrecognized H. erectus group that would differ in molecular and morphological aspects from the currently known H. erectus specimens, a hypothesis that we consider unlikely (Supplementary Note 2) but cannot outright reject, or belong to a non-erectus group, possibly related to H. longi. Future morphological and proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region, as well as the availability of a growing number of Denisovan genomes and proteomes, could therefore provide additional frameworks to allow a more precise classification of the PA1796 specimen.

The H. erectus specimens from Baxian and Naxian caves extend the geographical and temporal extent of mainland Asian H. erectus well into the late Middle Pleistocene. Occupying rainforest environments12, these H. erectus populations probably co-existed in close spatial and temporal proximity to southern Asian Denisovans. Mainland Southeast Asia therefore appears as a key region to study the evolution, genetics and archaeologically visible behaviours of multiple sympatric hominin species.

The Baxian and Naxian hominin specimens were scanned using X-ray microtomography using the 225 kV micro-computed tomography scanner at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP, Beijing, China) according to the following parameters: 140 kV voltage, 120 µA, 0.5 angular increment one step and 360° of rotation. The final volumes were reconstructed with isotropic voxel sizes of 15.7–32.0 µm. A semi-automatic threshold-based segmentation was carried out in Avizo v.7.1 (FEI Visualization Sciences Group) and a volumetric reconstruction was then generated for each specimen. A full morphological description of each tooth can be found in Supplementary Note 1.

Dental surface models were imported in Geomagic Design v. X 64 (3D Systems, Rock Hill) to separate the crown from the tooth roots. The crown and roots were digitally isolated at the cervix using the cervix-best-fit plane as a reference51. Five variables were then measured or calculated: (1) Ve, the volume of the enamel cap (mm3); (2) SEDJ, the surface area of the EDJ (mm2); (3) Vcdp, the volume of the crown dentine and pulp (mm3); (4) 3DAET, 3D average enamel thickness (Ve/SEDJ; mm)52; (5) 3DRED, the ratio of 3D average enamel thickness to 3D average dentine thickness (Ve1/3/Vcdp1/3 × 10)53.

Diffeomorphic surface matching was applied to analyse the EDJ shape of the least worn teeth from Baxian and Naxian caves (methodological details are provided in Supplementary Note 2). This landmark-free, mesh-based approach was previously demonstrated to efficiently distinguish the EDJ of various hominin species6,22,27. Owing to occlusal wear, the apex of the dentine horns of some of the specimens had to be reconstructed before the analysis (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 18 and 21). We first confirmed that the EDJ of the Baxian and Naxian specimens differed from that of Pongo and belonged to Homo (which was also confirmed independently by palaeoproteomics). We then compared the Baxian and Naxian EDJs to those of H. erectus s.l., H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens. The H. erectus sample includes dental remains from African and Asia that are regarded by some as belonging to H. ergaster and H. erectus s.s. (Supplementary Table 3). We indicated the labels of the H. erectus specimens in Fig. 2 to show the distribution of the African and Asian material in the morphospace. Canonical variate analyses were conducted and the Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as the Denisovan molar from Tam Ngu Hao 2 (ref. 6), were projected a posteriori into the canonical variate analysis morphospace. Typicality probabilities were computed for the Naxian and Baxian teeth to provide a quantitative estimation of their most likely taxonomic attribution.

For Naxian cave, fauna and hominin specimens were sampled using a handheld drill with a diamond-tipped drill bit, resulting in between 10 mg and 97 mg of powder for the faunal samples and up to 6 mg of hominin dental enamel. For Baxian cave, dentine was obtained using a handheld drill (36.5 and 43.2 mg of powder), while the dental enamel was sampled using an acid etch. All sampling and extraction steps were conducted in ancient molecular laboratories regularly used for ancient DNA and/or ancient protein analysis, including standard procedures to prevent contamination from occurring in the sampling and extraction environments, including wearing full body suits, hairnets, multiple layers of nitrile gloves, footies and positive air pressure.

Dental enamel extracts for Naxian cave were generated using 5% HCl, following previously published protocols31,54. Likewise, dental enamel extracts from the acid etching of the Baxian cave specimens followed previously published protocols54. The dentine samples of fauna from Naxian cave were extracted using a variant on previously published EDTA-based protocols55. For Baxian cave, the hominin dentine extractions followed a HCl-based protocol commonly used for ZooMS analysis, but with modifications to separate protein fragments by size9,56. Full protein extraction protocols are provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Faunal extracts from Naxian cave were separated on the EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Hominin dental enamel extracts from Naxian cave were analysed on the Vanquish Neo UPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Dentine extracts from Baxian cave were first analysed on the Bruker Autoflex MaX MALDI-ToF MS instrument. Subsequent to the detection of collagen peptides, both the dentine and the dental enamel extracts from Baxian cave were analysed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) over a 120 min gradient. Blank extractions were included in all cases to monitor the existence of exogenous contaminants during the procedure.

Raw data files were searched separately by tissue type and cave site, using PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant in parallel. Initial searches in PEAKS revealed the possibility of a unique substitution in AMBN, while PEAKS and pFind informed on the composition of post-translational modifications (PTMs) that should be taken into account. After initial searches, final searches using an updated protein sequence database and updated PTM information for dental enamel and the full human proteome for dentine were performed (further details are provided in Supplementary Note 3).

Protein deamidation was calculated according to a previous study for MaxQuant data57. Other PTM ratio analyses were conducted by peptide-spectrum match spectral counts or peptide counts, unless indicated differently (applying to MaxQuant, pFind and/or PEAKS). Unipept analysis was carried out using all peptide matches against endogenous, dental-enamel-specific proteins58. As described above, a project-specific database was used for data analysis that includes protein sequence variation beyond that available within UniProt. As a result, Unipept analysis will not be able to match all peptides to the same taxonomic level as the one present in the protein sequence database used. Sequence reconstruction was performed for pFind, PEAKS and MaxQuant data jointly, resulting in a single protein sequence reconstruction for each specimen. Specifically, sequences from different search engines were overlaid for each specimen to generate a single protein consensus sequence. Amino acid positions where PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant disagreed with each other were not called, and reversed to ‘X’. Positions possibly phylogenetically informative were manually inspected, fragment ion series were checked and E values were assessed. Where necessary, positions potentially introducing invalid sequences were subsequently removed from the protein sequence reconstructions. The consensus sequences were subsequently aligned to a subset of the PaleoProPhyler database of hominid dental enamel sequences, which included four individuals from each of the genera Pongo, Gorilla and Pan, as well as three Neanderthals41,42,43, one Denisovan44 and three present-day H. sapiens from the sub-Saharan Yoruba population. We also added the dental enamel protein sequences for Homo antecessor29 and Penghu 1 (ref. 7) (a Denisovan individual) and carried out Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the Naxian–Baxian individuals using a combination of different proteins for each tree. The combinations are indicated in each figure (Extended Data Figs. 4–6 and Supplementary Figs. 33–43). The available H. erectus protein sequences from a single specimen (D4163) from Dmanisi, Georgia, were not included in the phylogenetic analysis carried out here because the phylogenetic position of the specimen could not be resolved in the original study29.

These fossils and their CT data are freely available to access for any researchers. #1348. Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa

From the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa said. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

Konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

The victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also says plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

Probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

Brilliant play from Oscar Bobb as he cuts inside on his left foot and bends a shot into the far bottom corner for the away side.

Treatment is needed for Zubimendi after he is caught on the nose by Barry.

Big chance for Everton. Garner whips a teasing cross into the box, Dewsbury-Hall meets it with his head on the run but the ball flies just wide of the post.

EvertonOFF Johnson, Mykolenko ON Dibling, Hackney

Tarkowski is the latest yellow card for Everton after a foul on Havertz.

Eze with a poor cross into the box. He fails to run back quickly and Arteta sprints to the edge of the touchline and goes berserk at the midfielder.

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

It is a lovely move with slick one-touch passing. The ball is fed to White making a run down the outside and he clips the ball to the far post for Gabriel to head home.

OFF Merino, Lewis-Skelly, GyokeresON Calafiori, Guimaraes, Havertz

Garner is booked for Everton now after barging into Merino off the ball.

Arteta is shown a yellow card for something. Not sure what for yet. But the Arsenal manager is looking to make some changes off the bench.

Arsenal have been guilty of overplaying today. Opting for the extra pass rather than taking a shot. The game is open at the moment and that makes things dangerous for the home side.

Yellow card for Lewis-Skelly after bringing down Johnson. Gabriel is back on the pitch and seems happy enough to continue.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Gabriel immediately raised his hand for medical attention after making that clearance. He really extended his leg to get the ball away. Looks to be in a lot of pain.

Latest corner from Arsenal after Eze’s shot is blocked by Rohl. Rice’s delivery into the near post is headed clear to Odegaard, who shoots ambitiously from distance and Pickford collects the ball comfortably.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

Before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

Yellow card for Mykolenko after he catches White wide on the right. Rice whips the ball in and Merino meets it with a flick goalwards but the ball goes over the bar.

That is the final touch of the half and the players are running off to get dry!

Big chance for Everton. White thinks he has time when he heads the ball back to Raya but he does not connect well and Barry is there to pick it up and he flicks a shot at goal but Raya reacts quickly to parry the ball.

Raya is penalised for taking too long with the ball and Everton have a cheap corner. Danger is cleared by Arsenal as they force Everton back into their half.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Madueke should do better. Rice finds him and the winger drives into the box. He takes a shot but drags a right-footed effort wide.

Chance for Arsenal. Rice finds space behind the Everton midfield and drives forward. He plays a pass to Lewis-Skelly, who lays it off to Eze. The England midfielder sidefoots a cross into the box but no one in an Arsenal shirt is there to meet it.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

George is looking lively for Everton. He tries to come inside and whip an effort to the far corner but the ball deflects wide.

From the corner, Gabriel clears off the line after Raya loses track of the ball.

Everton have responded impressively to the Konsa goal and have been the better team since falling behind. Midfielders Garner and Armstrong are growing into the game quite nicely.

Everton have responded well to going behind here. The early goal against them will have ripped up any plans to sit deep and play on the counter.

Set-pieces are back on the menu for Arsenal. Ezri Konsa’s first goal for the club is their first goal from a corner this season, which will come as a relief to set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. “Set piece again, ole ole,” sing the Arsenal fans. Arteta’s side had started the game on the front foot.

Arsenal had not scored from a corner this season... until now. Konsa breaks the deadlock after a melee in the box and his pokes the ball into the net.

A couple of early set pieces from Declan Rice. Everton do well to clear the danger. But have another one now...

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

After a minute’s applause in honour of Ken Friar, the match makes a prompt start at the Emirates.

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

“They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”

“Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz

Everton: Pickford, Tarkowski, O’Brien, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George, Barry, Garner, Mykolenko, JohnsonSubs: Travers, King, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Dibling, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Braiden Graham

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United manager was secretly filmed by a drone and posted online, sparking a major security breach at Carrington ahead of Sunday’s huge Premier League clash against Liverpool.

According to a report from The Sun, Pochettino’s inaugural full pitch session on Thursday was recorded from above by an unauthorized drone hovering over United’s training complex.

A 12-minute video in crystal-clear quality, complete with live commentary from the drone operator, has since been uploaded to YouTube by an account named CC OVERVIEW.

The leaked footage captures United’s first-team stars being put through sharp passing and pressing drills across one of Carrington’s main pitches.

Pochettino can also be seen actively stopping play to deliver detailed tactical instructions to individual players before gathering the entire squad together for an animated center-circle team talk as he begins implementing his high-intensity philosophy.

The intrusion is certain to frustrate Pochettino and United’s security staff, particularly given the timing of the leak.

Having only touched down in Manchester on Wednesday following the conclusion of his tenure with the United States national team, the 54-year-old Argentine has just days to prepare an 18th-placed United side for a daunting clash against rivals Liverpool.

The Red Devils have managed only one win in 10 league outings so far this season. However, Liverpool are yet to win at home his season.

With Pochettino working under tight time constraints to drill new tactical patterns and surprise Andoni Iraola’s side on Merseyside, having 12 minutes of private preparation broadcast publicly on YouTube is the last distraction he needed.

#1345. Harry Kane up for ANOTHER prize alongside three England team-mates - as Globe Soccer Awards voting opens ahead of glitzy Dubai ceremony

Published: 04:11 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 03:04 EST, 19 November 2026

Harry Kane is one of the main contenders for the prestigious Best Men's Player prize at the Globe Soccer Awards - and you can vote for the winner.

The Ballon d'Or king is joined by England team-mates Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice, and Bukayo Saka in the category.

Meanwhile, Lionesses star Alessia Russo is the sole English representative in contention for the Best Women's Player honour.

Voting is now open across 12 categories, with the awards to be handed out at a glitzy ceremony in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on December 28.

The Globe Soccer Awards began in 2010 and have since become popular among fans worldwide, with more than 100 million votes cast in some years.

Last year's winner Ousmane Dembele is also in the running for Best Men's Player, with Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal, and Kylian Mbappe joining him in the 26-strong shortlist.

Harry Kane, pictured with the Ballon d'Or, is among the nominees for Best Men's PLayer at the Globe Soccer Awards

Voting is now open across 12 award categories ahead of a ceremony in Dubai in December

Erling Haaland won the Best Men's Player prize for 2023 and is in contention again

Premier League stars Erling Haaland, Bruno Fernandes, William Saliba, and Dominik Szoboszlai are also hoping to get their hands on the prize.

Mikel Arteta and Unai Emery are in the running for Best Coach, while Myles Lewis-Skelly and Nico O'Reilly are competing for the Emerging Player gong.

There are 14 categories, with a 'Career and Special Awards' section yet to see its talent announced.

Arsenal are hopefuls in the Best Club category for both men and women, with Aston Villa joining them in the former and Manchester City in the latter.

There will also be prizes for the best forward, midfielder, defender, and goalkeeper, and Fans' Historic Club, Best Sporting Director, and Best Agent.

Ronaldo, a serial winner at the ceremony, is defending his Best Middle East Player crown after winning his first Saudi Pro League title with Al-Nassr. Ivan Toney is among his rivals for that.

Fans are able to cast their votes until November 30, after which a jury including the likes of Antonio Conte and Luis Figo will also have their say.

It is an event of truly global interest, with supporters from more than 225 countries having cast votes in previous editions.

'We are incredibly proud to return for our third consecutive year as title partner of the GLOBE SOCCER Awards,' said Adil Taqi, CEO of title sponsor BEYOND Developments.

'Our continued partnership reflects BEYOND Developments’ commitment to connecting with an international audience through shared passions and experiences.

'Football brings people together across cultures and borders, resonating with our belief in pushing boundaries and aiming higher, a mindset shared by the players, coaches and clubs who will be honoured this December. We are proud to stand alongside an event that unites the global football family.'

Fans are able to vote via the Globe Soccer App.

Manchester United have been urged to pursue Fulham defender Calvin Bassey, with a potential £ 40 million-plus transfer emerging as an attractive option for new manager Mauricio Pochettino ahead of the January window.

The Red Devils are expected to strengthen their defensive options when the transfer market reopens, having endured a difficult start to the Premier League campaign. Pochettino will be keen to address the club’s defensive vulnerabilities and bring in players who can adapt to his preferred style of football.

According to a report via TEAMtalk, former United striker Louis Saha believes Bassey would be a smart addition to the squad, having established himself as a dependable performer at Fulham.

The Nigerian international has impressed with his physical presence, defensive awareness and ability to operate in multiple positions. His experience in English football could also make him an appealing option for the Old Trafford hierarchy.

Saha believes the 26-year-old has demonstrated impressive consistency over the last few seasons and could bring much-needed stability to United’s backline.

The former striker also highlighted defensive shortcomings in the current squad, suggesting Bassey could offer greater reliability at the back.

Saha said: “Who would he be competing with at Manchester United? The current defenders tend to make mistakes and get injured quite often, which doesn’t provide the stability a team under this much pressure needs.

“Hopefully, we find the right player, and Bassey could be a smart addition.”

United have several areas requiring attention, but recruiting a dependable defender should be among Pochettino’s immediate priorities. Bassey’s versatility and Premier League experience make him an intriguing candidate, and a January move could benefit both parties.

#1342. Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses1,2. Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum, with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

The genus Hordeum comprises approximately 33 species and is widely distributed across the temperate regions of Eurasia and the Americas1,2,3. Hordeum is classified into two subgenera based on cytogenetic evidence: one containing the H and Xu genomes and the other containing the I and Xa genomes4. The basic chromosome number is seven, and, although most species are diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid taxa have also been described. Cultivated barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the best known and most extensively studied species, as it represents one of the earliest domesticated cereal crops. Today, barley is the world’s fourth most important grain, valued for its use in food, animal feed and brewing5. Cultivated barley and its wild progenitor (H. vulgare subsp. spontaneum) constitute a single inter-fertile gene pool, allowing for frequent gene flow between wild and cultivated forms6. This primary gene pool has long been exploited by breeders to introduce desirable traits6. Hordeum bulbosum has contributed valuable disease resistance genes through introgression7,8,9,10 due to its ability to hybridize directly with cultivated barley. The other Hordeum species are not domesticated but have important ecological and agricultural roles in ecosystem stability, environmental adaptation and forage use11,12,13,14,15. Together, Hordeum is both an agronomically important genus and a powerful model for studying crop evolution, environmental adaptation and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. Factors such as incomplete lineage sorting, recurrent hybridization and gene flow partly obscure species boundaries, leaving major evolutionary questions unresolved1,2,4,16,17. Recent barley pangenomes have substantially advanced our understanding of genomic variation within cultivated barley and its closest relatives10,18,19. However, these studies were largely confined to two species (H. vulgare and H. bulbosum) and therefore could not resolve genome-wide evolutionary processes operating across the genus, including the origin of large-scale structural variation, ancient hybridization, polyploid genome evolution and the diversification of regulatory loci. Extending comparative genomic analyses to encompass the entire genus is therefore essential to capture the full breadth of diversity within the Hordeum gene pool and to facilitate both evolutionary studies and the effective utilization of wild germplasm for barley improvement. Pangenomics now offers comprehensive resources to address such complexity. In crops such as tomato, potato, maize, grapevine, citrus and cotton, genus-level pangenomes have uncovered extensive structural variations, gene presence–absence and evolutionary dynamics20,21,22,23,24. Investigating structural variations helps to explain evolutionary processes and can inform crop breeding strategies25. However, the full extent of structural variation within Hordeum remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies representing all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. This comparative genomic framework provides a view of structural and regulatory genome evolution across the genus, yielding new insights into genome evolution and establishing a foundation for the utilization of wild diversity in barley improvement.

To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–25). The dataset comprises 22 diploid accessions, 4 tetraploid accessions and 1 hexaploid accession. Twenty-four genome sequences were assembled using PacBio HiFi accurate long reads and Hi-C data (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Figs. 26–28), using the TRITEX pipeline26,27. The sequence assemblies of H. vulgare and H. bulbosum were sourced from our previous work10,28. The previously published chromosome-level assembly of Hordeum marinum H559 (ref. 29) was updated using the TRITEX pipeline, and previously published transcriptome data, Bionano optical maps and Hi-C data of Hordeum erectifolium NGB6816 were used30. The average contig N50 of the assemblies is 39.24 Mb. Assembly sizes range from 2.90 Gb to 4.48 Gb (mean, 3.92 Gb) in diploid species and from 7.49 Gb to 8.56 Gb (mean, 8.16 Gb) in tetraploid species, whereas the single hexaploid genome has an assembly size of 10.90 Gb. Chloroplast genome assemblies range from 136,335 bp to 137,079 bp (mean, 136,840 bp) (Supplementary Table 1). High assembly quality is supported by an average long terminal repeat (LTR) assembly index (LAI) of 14.79, a consensus quality value (QV) of 67.30 and k-mer completeness of 97.22% (Supplementary Table 4). For the heterozygous diploid species H. bulbosum, the two phased haplotypes were designated as Hap1 and Hap2. For polyploid species, independently assembled chromosome sets derived from different ancestral genomes were defined as subgenomes and denoted as Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 according to their phylogenetic relationships with diploid progenitor lineages (Fig. 1a). To assess the gene content in the Hordeum pangenome, we annotated all genomes using transcriptome data (Methods and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). A gene consolidation method was applied to ensure high comparability of gene predictions, including those for Hordeum parodii (6x) and Hordeum gussoneanum (4x). The number of high-confidence gene models identified ranges from 35,573 for diploid Hordeum murinum to 94,943 for hexaploid H. parodii (Supplementary Table 7). We assessed the quality of the Hordeum gene annotations using BUSCO (v5.8.0) with the poales_odb12 dataset, comprising 6,282 near-universal single-copy orthologues from Poales. On average, 97.35% of BUSCO genes were identified as complete, 0.69% as fragmented and 1.84% as missing (Supplementary Table 7). Independent benchmarking with OMArk and PSAURON further confirmed the high completeness and overall quality of the gene annotations (Supplementary Table 7). Transposable element (TE) annotation using the panEDTA pipeline31 revealed that transposons constituted on average 86.12% of the genome, ranging from 83.27% to 90.35% (Supplementary Table 8).

a, Phylogenetic tree of Hordeum species. Sorghum bicolor, Oryza sativa, Brachypodium distachyon and Triticum monococcum were used as outgroups. Divergence times were inferred using 4DTV sites from genome-wide single-copy genes after excluding genomic regions with strong phylogenetic discordance (nRF > 0.21) identified in Extended Data Fig. 6c. Coloured rectangles represent different genome groups. Hap1 and Hap2 represent phased haplotypes of heterozygous diploid H. bulbosum, and Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 indicate distinct ancestral subgenomes in polyploid species. The background colours represent the genome groups of the species in the following order from top to bottom: I, Xa, H, Xu and outgroup species. b, GENESPACE synteny plot among 34 Hordeum haplomes and four outgroup genomes. Grey bars represent chromosomes arranged by genomic position. For visualization purposes, the chromosomes of the smaller outgroup genomes (S. bicolor, O. sativa and B. distachyon) were proportionally enlarged by a factor of five. c, Dot plot comparisons of chromosome 4H across genomes diverged at different times. Two species were randomly selected from each phylogenetic node for sequence alignment (Supplementary Table 11). Six representative comparisons are shown, with the remaining comparisons presented in Extended Data Fig. 3a. The number displayed at the top of each alignment represents the estimated divergence time between the species shown on the x axis and those shown on the y axis.

Based on the annotated gene sets of all species, we constructed a gene-based Hordeum pangenome. Overall, 42.4% of genes were classified as core genes, 56.5% as shell genes and 1.1% as cloud genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). Gene ontology enrichment analysis showed that phosphorylation- and kinase-related functions were enriched among core genes, ATP and RNA binding were enriched among shell genes, and defence response and oxidative stress response were enriched among cloud genes (Supplementary Fig. 29). Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes are key components of the plant immune system and have essential roles in resistance to fungal and other pathogens32,33. A map of their diversity is critical for advancing our understanding of disease resistance mechanisms in crops. Analysis of NLR genes revealed that I genome species contain significantly more NLR genes than the other Hordeum genome groups (Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). To further characterize this diversity, we constructed an NLR pangenome across Hordeum haploid genome equivalents (haplomes), comprising 800 orthogroups, of which 13.75% were classified as core, 27.75% as shell and 58.50% as cloud gene families (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In addition, NLR gene clusters were significantly less abundant on chromosomes 4H and 5H than on the remaining chromosomes (Wilcoxon test, P < 2.2 × 10−16) (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Similarly, genome-wide analyses of pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins and mitochondrial transcription termination factors (mTERFs) revealed significant expansions of restorer-of-fertility-like (RFL) subgroups in the I and Xa genome groups relative to the H and Xu genome groups. Because RFL proteins are involved in fertility restoration in plants carrying cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)34, these expansions suggest that the smaller RFL repertoires of the H and Xu genome groups are derived rather than ancestral (Supplementary Fig. 30a–e and Supplementary Table 9). Expansion of RFL-PPRs was most pronounced in the I genome group, whereas RFL-mTERFs were significantly expanded in both the I and Xa genome groups. Notably, RFL-mTERF genes clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6H exhibited extensive copy-number variation between Xa–I and H–Xu genome groups (t-test, P = 5.2 × 10−6) (Supplementary Fig. 30f). This region includes the Rfm3 locus, which partially restores fertility in plants carrying the msm1 cytoplasm used in hybrid barley breeding35 (Supplementary Fig. 30g).

To assess the feasibility of graph-based pangenome analyses across highly diverged Hordeum genomes, we constructed a pangenome graph using Progressive Cactus and hal2vg, comprising 2.53 billion nodes and 3.46 billion edges (68.7 Gb). Approximately 68% of nodes represented single-base variants, illustrating the extensive sequence divergence captured by the graph. Although computationally intensive tasks such as indexing remained infeasible (Methods), we successfully performed global analyses of core, shell and cloud sequence content, graph saturation, sequence conservation and variant diversity (Supplementary Figs. 31–34). These results demonstrate both the potential of graph-based approaches for genus-wide comparative genomics and the need for more scalable methods for graph exploration and interpretation.

Previous studies have inferred the evolutionary relationships among Hordeum species from plastome and partial gene sequences1,17. However, the relationships among some species remained weakly supported. In this study, we reconstructed a maximum-likelihood tree using a genome-wide single-copy gene set. Unlike previous phylogenies1,17, our species tree resolved all major evolutionary relationships with maximum bootstrap support, particularly among the recently diverged I-genome species (Supplementary Fig. 35). To further evaluate the robustness of these relationships, we reconstructed an independent coalescent-based species tree using ASTRAL-Pro3 (Supplementary Fig. 36), which integrates individual maximum-likelihood gene trees, and a genome-wide phylogeny inferred by CASTER from whole-genome multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38). We also estimated the divergence times of these species using fourfold degenerate third-codon transversion (4DTV) sites, excluding genomic regions identified as putatively derived from ancient hybridization (Supplementary Table 13). We estimated the divergence time between H and Xu at 10.3 million years ago (Ma), whereas I and Xa diverged around 9 Ma. The crown-group age of Hordeum dates back approximately 12.27 Ma (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 10). The chromosomes of Triticeae species exhibit high collinearity at their distal chromosome regions36, which is also the case in Hordeum (Fig. 1b). However, when aligned, the proximal regions show substantial loss of collinearity and highly fragmented alignments. Whole-genome comparisons across Hordeum species revealed that chromosomal rearrangements accumulated progressively with evolutionary divergence, contributing to the loss of collinearity and increasingly fragmented alignments in proximal chromosomal regions (Fig.1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 39–44 and Supplementary Table 11). Quantification of reverse-orientation alignments across all Hordeum haplomes further demonstrated that putative inversions accumulated significantly more rapidly in proximal than in distal chromosome regions during Hordeum evolution (Supplementary Fig. 45). Among the seven chromosomes, chromosome 4H exhibited the most extensive loss of proximal collinearity (Supplementary Table 12). Recently diverged species retained strong chromosome-scale collinearity despite the presence of numerous structural variants, whereas comparisons between the deeply diverged H–Xu and Xa–I genome groups (more than 9 Ma) showed almost complete fragmentation of proximal collinearity (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 39–44). To estimate the size of non-collinear regions, we applied normalized coverage to identify these regions in species that diverged more than 9 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d, Supplementary Figs. 46–50 and Methods). In total, we determined the genome-wide distribution of non-collinear regions across chromosomes in Hordeum, with a cumulative size of 855 Mb identified in the H. vulgare genome (Supplementary Table 12). Given the central role of TEs in genome evolution, we compared TE composition between proximal and distal chromosome regions. Proximal regions contained a significantly higher proportion of TEs than distal regions (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10), primarily due to an increased abundance of LTR/Gypsy retrotransposons (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Fig. 51). Together with the accumulation of large chromosomal rearrangements, these observations motivated a ‘stretch and twist’ model describing two complementary processes underlying the progressive loss of collinearity. The stretch component represents alignment displacement caused by TE amplification, whereas the twist component represents large-scale chromosomal rearrangements driven by structural variation (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

In contrast to the dynamic structural variations found in proximal regions, the distal regions displayed more conserved, shared structural variations. This highlights that the extensive loss of collinearity in proximal regions precludes reliable identification of structural variants across more distantly related Hordeum species. Notably, large structural variations in the distal regions were predominantly inversions. On chromosomes 3H and 7H, we identified two large inversions spanning nearly the entire chromosome and present in multiple species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In total, 1,407 inversions larger than 2 Mb were identified across Hordeum species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). The construction of a comprehensive inversion map revealed six inversions on chromosome 1H that were unexpectedly shared across divergent phylogenetic lineages (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5). We hypothesized that these large-scale structural variations might have originated from introgression events involving extensive chromosomal segments. We constructed a phylogenetic tree using the single-copy gene set from these regions to test this hypothesis. The resulting tree, resolved with maximum bootstrap support, confirmed that these structural variations are shared between one clade of the I genome group and the H–Xu genome groups (Fig. 2b). Moreover, 10 extant diploid Hordeum species diversified within 1.68 million years following the inferred hybridization event, whereas no comparable radiation occurred in other phylogenetic lineages during the same period (Figs. 1a and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 5). Notably, the alternative phylogenetic topology extends across contiguous chromosomal regions of approximately 200 Mb rather than isolated loci, indicating the inheritance of chromosome-scale haplotypes that are more consistent with ancient introgression than with stochastic gene tree discordance or incomplete lineage sorting.

The remaining genome comparisons are shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. To identify additional signatures of ancient hybridization across the genus, we developed a genome-wide scanning approach based on local phylogenetic discordance among single-copy genes. The single-copy gene set was partitioned into sliding windows, and normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distance was calculated between local phylogenetic trees and the genome-wide species tree (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Peaks in nRF values indicate genomic regions with phylogenetic histories that deviate from the species tree and therefore represent candidate introgression events. Here, we define hybridization footprints as large chromosomal segments shared among multiple descendant species that consistently exhibit an alternative phylogenetic relationship relative to the genome-wide species tree. Using an empirical threshold of 0.21 derived from the genome-wide nRF distribution to distinguish discordance peaks from background variation (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 52), we recovered the chromosome 1H hybridization signal, validating the genome-wide scanning approach. Additionally, we detected more than ten consecutive windows with strong phylogenetic discordance signals at multiple regions (Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 52). To further explore the underlying causes of these inconsistencies, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the single-copy gene sets from these regions (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f, Supplementary Figs. 53–58 and Supplementary Table 13). Regions in which local phylogenies consistently supported a specific alternative relationship across a large chromosomal segment were interpreted as evidence of ancient hybridization. By comparing the regions that exhibited phylogenetic discordance with the whole-genome tree, we identified two large-scale segmental exchanges occurring within Hordeum jubatum, with maximum bootstrap support (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f and Supplementary Table 13). Surprisingly, this large-scale segmental exchange explains the major duplication and deletion pattern previously identified on chromosome 5H relative to the H. vulgare reference genome (Supplementary Figs. 12, 56, 59 and 60). The exchanged regions in the two H. jubatum subgenomes are each more closely related to different ancestral genomes, indicating that the apparent duplication and deletion resulted from ancestral segmental exchange rather than independent copy-number changes. (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum, extensive segmental exchanges were detected between the two subgenomes on chromosomes 2, 5 and 7 (Extended Data Fig. 6e, Supplementary Figs. 53, 55 and 57 and Supplementary Table 13). In the allohexaploid H. parodii, subgenome 1 carried a large chromosomal segment on chromosome 7 derived from Hordeum stenostachys, whereas subgenomes 2 and 3 exhibited an additional segmental exchange on chromosome 4 (Extended Data Fig. 6f, Supplementary Figs. 54, 55 and 58 and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these megabase-scale structural variants preserve signatures of ancient interspecific hybridization and large-scale chromosomal exchange that are not evident from genome-wide phylogenies alone, providing new insights into the complex evolutionary history of Hordeum.

Genetic variation is essential for species evolution. Beyond sexual reproduction, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) serves as an evolutionary shortcut for acquiring novel genes. Traditionally considered rare in vascular plants, genomic advances have revealed widespread occurrences of HGT, challenging prior assumptions37,38. Our previous research demonstrated extensive HGT in Hordeum. Notably, species within section stenostachys (I genome; 16 out of 22 diploid species) possess ribosomal DNA (rDNA) acquired from grasses in the subfamily Panicoideae (for example, Panicum, Paspalum and Setaria)39,40. The oldest transfers (from Panicum), estimated to have occurred between 5 and 1.7 Ma, resulted in large genomic insertions on chromosome 5H, some spanning over 400 kb and containing TEs and protein-coding genes41. Here, we identified Panicoideae-derived nuclear genes across 20 diploid Hordeum species, with H. vulgare serving as a negative control39,41. Our analysis revealed 611 foreign genes that corresponded to 126 orthogroups, predominantly matching Paspalum (63%) and Panicum (22%) (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 14 and 15). The extent of HGT varied, with Hordeum flexuosum carrying the highest number of foreign genes (68 genes corresponding to 43 orthogroups) (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These findings align with studies indicating that grasses frequently exchange genetic material42,43. HGT frequency correlates with Hordeum phylogeny, with Mediterranean and West Asian species exhibiting fewer transferred genes than their South American counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that HGT has a cumulative impact on eukaryotic evolution44. The presence of a single panicoid gene in H. bulbosum and H. murinum can be explained by the introgression of chromosomal segment 1H from I genome species, rather than by an early HGT event predating the diversification of Hordeum (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6c). Chromosomal mapping indicates that horizontally transferred genes are distributed across all seven Hordeum chromosomes, with chromosome 5H carrying the largest number (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These genes are significantly enriched in the distal regions of chromosome arms. Although distal regions generally contain higher local gene densities, negative binomial regression analysis showed that gene density explains only a small fraction of the observed variation in HGT abundance (pseudo-R2 = 0.034; Supplementary Fig. 61), indicating that higher gene density alone cannot account for the distal enrichment of HGT genes. Although co-transfer of genes remains uncertain, previous research suggests that large fragments of foreign DNA may be transferred together41,43. A substantial fraction (82 out of 126) of Panicoideae-derived orthogroups lack native Hordeum homologues, indicating novel gene acquisition. Functional annotation suggests that these genes may have roles in key physiological processes such as auxin transport, light response and transcription regulation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis detected at least one expressed HGT gene in 73 out of 126 orthogroups (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 16). The potential adaptive significance of these genes warrants further investigation. Our genus-wide analysis establishes Hordeum as a model system for studying the evolutionary impact of HGT.

The genome assembly sizes of Hordeum species range from 2.90 Gb to 10.9 Gb and are highly correlated with previous flow-cytometric estimates45 (Fig. 3a). After accounting for the direct effects of polyploidization, the haplomes exhibit pseudomolecule sizes ranging from 2.85 Gb to 4.68 Gb. Apart from a 19 Mb duplication detected in the subgenome of H. jubatum, no large duplication events were identified (Supplementary Figs. 59–60). A strong correlation was observed between total TE content and haplome size (Fig. 3b), confirming that TE accumulation has significantly contributed to genome size variation in Hordeum. LTR retrotransposons were identified as the primary drivers of these changes, although DNA transposons also had a role (Fig. 3c). Correlation analyses of individual transposon superfamilies showed that multiple TE families contributed to genome size variation, although overall TE abundance remained the strongest predictor of haplome size (Supplementary Fig. 62a). We selected transposons annotated in the TREP database with an average content above 20 Mb and examined their variation across different Hordeum haplomes. These TE families clearly differentiated the major evolutionary lineages of Hordeum (Supplementary Fig. 62b). To investigate lineage-specific TE dynamics in greater detail, we focused on three LTR retrotransposon families (BARE1, Sabrina and BAGY2) and used TEpop46 to reconstruct their diversification histories. TE subfamilies correspond closely to the major Hordeum clades (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), demonstrating lineage-specific amplification histories that contributed to genome size evolution.

Each dot represents one retrotransposon; colours indicate estimated insertion times (Ma). e, Distribution of insertion times of full-length LTR elements in H. jubatum, H. californicum and Hordeum roshevitzii. H. californicum and H. roshevitzii are the respective diploid progenitors of subgenomes 1 and 2 in H. jubatum1. f, Inference of post-allopolyploidization TE insertion dynamics in tetraploid H. murinum subsp. murinum (BCC 2009) based on full-length LTR/Copia elements shared between subgenomes. Subgenome-derived TEs represent TE insertions detected in one subgenome that are shared with the other subgenome but absent from the corresponding diploid progenitor, reflecting TE accumulation after subgenome fusion.
