To investigate TE evolution following polyploidization, we compared the TE landscapes of three independently formed tetraploid genomes with those of their diploid progenitors. The three polyploid species exhibited distinct evolutionary trajectories. In H. murinum, TE expansion was minimal (Extended Data Fig. 8c and Supplementary Table 17). In H. jubatum, both subgenomes were smaller than their diploid progenitors (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 17). By contrast, Hordeum secalinum experienced extensive TE proliferation, resulting in substantial genome expansion (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Table 17). Notably, LTR/Gypsy elements showed the greatest expansion relative to the diploid progenitors and therefore contributed most to genome expansion in H. secalinum (Supplementary Table 17). Additionally, the Vagabond TE family showed renewed activity following tetraploidization, with significantly higher activity in the tetraploid genome than in either its diploid progenitors or the alternative subgenome (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Figs. 63 and 64). To avoid bias introduced by large segmental exchanges between subgenomes, we excluded genomic regions inferred to originate from ancient hybridization before estimating TE insertion ages (Supplementary Table 13 and Supplementary Fig. 65). Although subgenome differentiation alone does not permit precise dating of tetraploid formation, post-polyploid TE dynamics can be reconstructed from TE insertions. Specifically, we inferred the timing of subgenome fusion from the insertion ages of full-length TEs shared exclusively between subgenomes but absent from their respective diploid progenitors (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 8f,g and Supplementary Figs. 65 and 66). These shared insertions must have occurred after polyploid formation, thereby providing temporal information on the origin of the polyploid genomes and subsequent TE activity. Our findings underscore that TE content is the primary determinant of genome size variation in Hordeum. Tetraploidization does not always lead to genome expansion relative to diploid ancestors; we also observed genome contraction. Nevertheless, post-polyploid LTR insertions provided an independent estimate of the timing of polyploid formation and new insights into the evolutionary history of tetraploid and hexaploid Hordeum genomes.

Whole-genome MSAs provide a framework for investigating sequence conservation and divergence across species. We therefore generated a whole-genome MSA of Hordeum haplomes using Progressive Cactus47. In total, we identified 170.4 Mb of shared aligned sequences across the Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 9a). As expected, rapidly evolving pericentromeric regions showed fewer alignments, whereas chromosome distal ends exhibited higher alignment densities (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The rapid contraction of these alignments is probably due to substantial reshaping of Hordeum genomes by TE activity over the past 12 million years. To further investigate sequence conservation across different functional genomic regions, we analysed open chromatin regions identified by assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq) together with annotated genomic features in eight Hordeum haplomes (Supplementary Table 18). Untranslated region sequences were the most highly conserved non-coding regions and were lost at a slower rate before the divergence of barley and wheat. By contrast, open chromatin regions exhibited a loss pattern similar to introns, whereas promoter regions underwent more rapid turnover (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Additionally, we used phastCons to identify 74.7 Mb of conserved elements across Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Among all conserved bases, 69.0% overlapped annotated genes and 6.0% overlapped open chromatin regions. Conversely, 44.7% of annotated gene bases and 31.9% of open chromatin bases overlapped conserved elements. Conserved elements were significantly enriched in both annotated genes (odds ratio = 138.0) and open chromatin regions (odds ratio = 27.4), with substantially stronger enrichment in genes, indicating stronger evolutionary constraint on coding sequences than on regulatory regions (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

Overall, our findings indicate that regulatory elements undergo substantially faster evolutionary turnover than coding sequences, generating extensive regulatory variation that may provide a valuable source of alleles for barley improvement. By contrast, the high conservation of coding genes provides opportunities for comparative functional analyses and cross-species transfer of biological knowledge.

In cultivated barley, spring and winter growth habits are largely determined by the vernalization genes VERNALIZATION 1 (VRN1), a MADS-box transcription factor, and VERNALIZATION 2 (VRN2), which is encoded by a cluster of zinc-finger/CCT (ZCCT) genes. In winter barley, prolonged cold induces VRN1 expression, which represses VRN2 and thereby permits flowering48,49. Flowering of winter varieties requires repression of VRN2 by cold-induced VRN1 (ref. 49). By contrast, spring barleys often carry deletions in the first intron of VRN1 and lack VRN2, eliminating their vernalization requirement50,51,52. Intermediate facultative types combine the vernalization-sensitive VRN1 with a non-functional VRN2 locus. It remains largely unexplored how wild Hordeum species regulate flowering across diverse climates.

Examining VRN1 in Hordeum genomes revealed extensive variation in the promoter and the regulatory first intron (5.7 kb to 19.5 kb) caused by TEs (Supplementary Table 19). To assess the functional effect of this variation, we recorded flowering time of 14 wild Hordeum species and 4 barley controls under non-vernalizing conditions with a 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Notably, Hordeum cordobense and Hordeum muticum flowered rapidly (approximately 61 days), surpassing spring barley cultivars (Fig. 4a). Both species share a unique 79-bp deletion in VRN1 intron 1 critical region51, suggesting a role in reducing the vernalization requirement (Extended Data Fig. 11b). All species contained the VRN2 locus with one to seven ZCCT copies (Supplementary Table 19). A key finding was an inverted repeat of two ZCCT genes in H. cordobense, Hordeum californicum, H. muticum and H. jubatum (Supplementary Fig. 67). Because inverted repeats may trigger RNA interference (RNAi)53, we expected silencing of VRN2 and a spring-type phenotype. Surprisingly, only H. cordobense and H. muticum flowered early (Fig. 4a,c and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Detailed analysis of H. cordobense revealed a non-functional ZCCT-1 owing to a premature stop codon, and the absence of a polyadenylation signal in the ZCCT-2/ZCCT-3 inverted repeat linker, enabling read-through transcription (detected as an aberrant mRNA transcript), hairpin RNA formation and small RNA production (Fig. 4b,d, Extended Data Fig. 11c and Supplementary Fig. 68). Winter-type H. californicum carried additional functional ZCCT copies and a polyadenylation signal in the inverted repeat linker that probably prevented RNAi, thus maintaining the VRN2 repressive function (Fig. 4b,e). This aligns with the expression of VRN1, VRN2 and their target FLOWERING LOCUS T1 (FT1) in the analysed species (Fig. 4f). These findings highlight that genetic diversity shapes vernalization in Hordeum. The studied spring-like accessions carry the 79-bp VRN1 deletion alongside disrupted or silenced VRN2, whereas winter-like genotypes retain functional ZCCT copies. Together, our results indicate that adaptation to spring growth habit in wild Hordeum species has targeted the same genes and variant types as in cultivated barley, pointing to conserved mechanisms of flowering-time adaptation.

The glume is a distinctive floral organ in the grass family, which lacks a direct counterpart in dicotyledonous plants54. It appears as one or multiple pairs of bract-like structures subtending single or multiple fertile florets. Glume size and shape vary widely, from large lemma-like structures in Triticum species to rudimentary axillary buds in Oryza. In wild grasses, glume morphology influences seed dispersal, reproductive success and defence against biotic stress55. In cultivated cereals, domestication has favoured reduced glume size and roughness, facilitating easier threshing. In Hordeum, each floret possesses a pair of glumes positioned on the periaxial side, with considerable variation in length, width and awn extension across species (Fig. 5a). Transcriptomic profiling of five diploid species carrying the I genome (H. erectifolium, Hordeum pusillum, Hordeum intercedens H. stenostachys and Hordeum euclaston) identified spike-specific genes expressed in young spikes at early (Waddington stages 3–6 (W3–6)) and late (W9–10) developmental stages56 (Supplementary Table 21). Genes were classified as spike-specific if their transcript abundance in the remaining 11 out of 13 analysed tissues was less than 5% of their combined expression in the 2 spike samples. Five genes were consistently expressed across species, suggesting conserved regulatory mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 12a and Supplementary Table 21). These genes encode a C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, an auxin response factor, a TCP transcription factor, a subtilisin protease (SBT) and a MADS-box transcription factor. Three were predominantly expressed during early spike development, one at later stages and one at both stages (Extended Data Fig. 12b). In rice, loss-of-function mutations in NONSTOP GLUMES1 (NSG1), the orthologue of the C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, result in uncontrolled glume growth57. Amino acid variations in this gene across Hordeum species along with glume variations suggested a relevance in regulating glume development (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 69). Mutations in its cultivated barley orthologue (EOG1) lead to the elongated outer glume (eog1) phenotype (Fig. 5b). These mutants develop enlarged glumes on the central fertile spikelet, with glume awns extending to lemma-awn length, giving the spike a brushy appearance (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed developmental divergence between wild-type and eog1 mutants as early as W3.5 (Fig. 5c). By integrating comparative genomics across Hordeum with tissue-specific expression data and cultivated barley mutant resources, we identify EOG1 as a conserved regulator of glume development.

The chromosome-scale genome assemblies presented here provide a foundation for investigating the evolutionary history of the genus Hordeum. Chromosome-scale resolution enables us to investigate how structural variations have shaped genome evolution, particularly in disrupting chromosomal collinearity. Traditionally, grass genomes were thought to possess relatively stable chromosome structures58; however, our findings challenge this assumption. Extensive structural variations and chromosomal rearrangements have contributed substantially to genomic divergence, ultimately resulting in the near-complete loss of collinearity in proximal regions. These rearrangements not only mark evolutionary divergence but also provide insights into the processes underlying speciation within Hordeum. Structural variations accumulated at markedly different rates across chromosome regions. Whereas proximal regions exhibit high variability, distal regions evolve more slowly. This uneven evolutionary rate has preserved footprints of ancient hybridization events across the genus, offering a historical record of interspecific gene flow. These findings provide empirical evidence for ancient hybridization and genome fusion during Hordeum evolution and establish a framework for identifying compatible genomic segments in future interspecific breeding efforts.

Nevertheless, whether the large inversions identified in this study contribute to adaptive evolution, reproductive isolation or other phenotypic consequences remains unknown and warrants future functional investigation. Whole-genome MSAs enabled us to compare genome-wide conservation across Hordeum species. Compared with animal genomes, which often display strong interspecies conservation, plant genomes—especially within rapidly evolving genera such as Hordeum—undergo dynamic changes driven by short generation times and rapid transposon expansion. These processes fuel the ongoing remodelling of plant genomes, resulting in high variability even among closely related taxa. Despite this rapid evolution, many genes remain conserved, whereas regulatory elements exhibit considerable turnover. This contrast offers unique opportunities: lineage-specific regulatory innovation can be harnessed for crop improvement, while core gene functions are retained. For example, regulatory elements associated with vernalization responses were found to vary across Hordeum species, suggesting that novel regulatory variants could be introduced into cultivated barley to fine-tune flowering behaviour. Beyond expanding genomic resources for Hordeum, this work provides a framework for investigating structural genome evolution, reconstructing complex evolutionary histories and harnessing genetic and regulatory diversity for barley improvement.

Plant material was obtained from genebanks at Institut für Pflanzgenetik und Kulturpflanzenforschung (IPK) Gatersleben, the US Department of Agriculture and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center. Accession numbers are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and high molecular weight (HMW) DNA was isolated from young leaf tissue according to published protocols10,60. Construction of HiFi libraries and Circular Consensus Sequencing using the PacBio Sequel IIe instrument (Pacific Biosciences) were essentially as described previously19. HiFi sequencing was done at IPK Gatersleben, Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory, Heinrich Heine University, Berry Genomics Co., Novogene and the University of Wisconsin Biotechnology Center DNA Sequencing Facility.

In situ Hi-C libraries were prepared from young seedlings according to the previously published protocol, using DpnII for the digestion of crosslinked chromatin. Libraries were prepared as described61. Samples were quantified62 and sequenced with standard protocols from Illumina using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina) at IPK Gatersleben and Novogene.

A clone of the same H. erectifolium individual plant that was sequenced using PacBio HiFi was used for the construction of the optical genome map (OGM). A total of 2.5 million nuclei, purified from young leaves by flow cytometry, were embedded in agarose miniplugs and treated with proteinase K, following the protocol of Šimková et al.63. A total of 525 ng of HMW DNA was directly labelled at DLE-1 recognition sites using the standard Bionano Prep Direct Label and Stain protocol (Bionano) and analysed on the Bionano Saphyr platform. The resulting dataset, comprising 1.5 Tb of single-molecule data with an N50 of 247 kb, provided approximately 341× coverage of the H. erectifolium genome. This dataset was used to generate a de novo OGM assembly using Bionano Solve software (v3.6.1_11162020) with the standard configuration file optArguments_nonhaplotype_noES_noCut_DLE1_saphyr.xml.

To improve the contiguity of the PacBio HiFi assembly, the automatic hybrid scaffold pipeline integrated in Bionano Solve was run using the OGM assembly. The default DLE-1 Hybrid Scaffold configuration file was applied with the ‘resolve conflict’ option for conflict resolution. Conflicts between the sequence assembly and the OGM were manually curated and the pipeline was subsequently re-run using a modified conflict_cut_status.txt file.

Plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and total RNA was isolated from different tissues and developmental stages (Supplementary Table 5) using the RNAeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) or with Trizol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. RNA-seq was performed on replicated bulk sample representing a specific developmental stage or tissue type. RNA-seq of individual samples and PacBio IsoSeq of RNA pools was performed as described previously10. Library construction and sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina RNA-seq) and PacBio Sequel IIe (instruments) was done at IPK Gatersleben, Biomarker Technologies (BMK), the Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Kazusa DNA Research Institute or Berry Genomics. The PacBio IsoSeq sequencing data was processed with the isoseq3 (v3.8.2) pipeline (PacBio - IsoSeq3, 2018/2024). The ploy-A tails were trimmed and concatenated transcripts removed with refine -require-polya-min-polya-length 12 teloprime.fasta. To generate non-redundant transcripts, we mapped the full-length non-concatenated reads were mapped to the genome with pbmm2 (v1.10.0) align -preset ISOSEQ -sort -bam-index CSI and redundant transcripts collapsed with isoseq3 collapse -do-not-collapse-extra-5exons.

PacBio HiFi reads were assembled using hifiasm (v0.13-r308 or v0.15.5-r350 or v0.16.1-r375)64. Pseudomolecules were constructed with the TRITEX pipeline26,27, and chimeric contigs or orientation errors were corrected based on manual inspection of Hi-C contact matrices. For allotetraploid species, subgenomes were phased using a previously developed haplotype-resolved genome assembly strategy10. The origin of the subgenomes and their potential ancestral contributors were previously investigated in detail by Brassac et al.1 To classify subgenomes in the polyploid genome, Mash (v2.3)65 was used to calculate pairwise chromosomal similarities between polyploid chromosomes and candidate ancestral genomes. The resulting distance matrix was used to infer subgenome origin and relationships. In species with high heterozygosity or outcrossing (H. brevisubulatum and H. murinum BBC2017), Hi-C data were incorporated during hifiasm (v0.15.5-r350)64 assembly to collapse haplotypes and assemble a representative haploid genome. Except for H. erectifolium, whose primary contigs were first hybrid-scaffolded using a Bionano optical map, followed by pseudomolecule construction with Hi-C data and the TRITEX pipeline30. Chloroplast genomes were assembled following previously published protocols10. HiFi reads were aligned to the barley cv. Morex chloroplast genome (GenBank accession EF115541) using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -ax map-hifi–secondary=no–sam-hit-only. Alignments with mapping quality <30 were discarded. Aligned reads were converted to FASTQ format using SAMtools (v1.16.1)67 and assembled with Canu (v2.1.1)68 in PacBio HiFi mode with genome sizes from 120 to 400 kb in 10-kb increments. Circular sequences were identified and trimmed using BEDTools (v2.30.0)69 and annotated with GeSeq70. Fully annotated assemblies were aligned to the Morex chloroplast genome using MUMmer4 (v4.0.0beta2)71, and start positions and orientations of the SSC region were adjusted to match the reference using seqkit (v0.9.1)72. k-mer frequencies were calculated using Jellyfish(v2.2.6)73 and analysed with findGSE(v1.94)74 to estimate genome characteristics. Assembly quality, including QV and k-mer completeness, was evaluated using Merqury(v1.3)75.

We performed de novo structural gene prediction, confidence classification and functional annotation, following the protocol described in Mascher et al.28. As evidences we used RNA-seq and IsoSeq data as described under above and Poales-filtered protein sequences downloaded from UniProt76 (July 2023). An additional consolidation step was carried out using the liftoff77 tool. In brief, all predicted gene models from one species were lifted over to all other genomes. Using Mikado78, we selected the best mapped gene models and unified all gene predictions accordingly. We classified predicted proteins into high and low-confidence categories. High-confidence proteins had over 80% coverage and were complete, either with significant hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP (https://trep-db.uzh.ch). Low-confidence proteins were incomplete with hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP, or were complete without hits in any database.

We benchmarked the annotations with BUSCO (v5.8.0)79 (dataset: poales_odb12), OMARK (omamer verision 2.1.0/omark v0.3.1)80 and psauron (v1.0.6)81.

Orthogroups based on the primary protein sequences from 27 annotated Hordeum accessions were calculated using Orthofinder (v2.5.5)82. The scripts for the calculation of core, shell and cloud genes are deposited in the repository at https://github.com/PGSB-HMGU/BPGv2. Core genes contain at least 1 gene model from all 27 compared accessions. Shell genes contain gene models from at least 2 Hordeum accessions and at most 26. Genes clustered with genes only from the same genotype were defined as cloud genes. Annotations of H. vulgare Morex and H. bulbosum were not included during the consolidation step. Therefore, to counteract any potential over- or under-presentation of these two species in any of the core, shell or cloud categories, we aligned all cloud genes for H. vulgare cv. Morex and H. bulbosum back to all other genomes and corrected for any missing genes. Gene Ontology-term enrichments were conducted with goatools (v1.4.4)83. Gene-based collinearity plots were drawn with GENESPACE84.

The RGAugury (v2.2)85 pipeline was used to identify from our annotation and classify nucleotide-binding site (NB-ARC) domain-encoding genes into different subgroups, based on domain and motif structures: TNL contain TIR, NBS and LRR domains; CNL contain CC, NBS and LRR domains; RNL contain RPW8, NBS and LRR domains; RN contain RPW8 and NBS domains only; NL contain NBS and LRR domains but lack TIR, CC and RPW8; TN contain TIR and NBS domains only; CN contain CC and NBS domains only; and NBS-only genes contain only the NBS domain. TIR, NBS, LRR, CC and RPW8 refer to the Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor-like, Nucleotide-Binding Site, Leucine-Rich Repeat, Coiled-Coil and Resistance to Powdery Mildew 8-like domains, respectively. An NLR gene cluster is defined based on the genomic proximity of NLR genes. Specifically, any two NLR genes located within 500 kb of each other are grouped into the same cluster by bedtools (v2.30.0)69. NLR genes were then grouped into clusters using bedtools (v2.30.0)69 merge with a maximum intergenic distance of 250 kb. Only clusters comprising no fewer than three NLR genes were retained. Pan-NLR analysis was performed based on orthogroups identified using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82 across all NLR genes. Core orthogroups are defined as orthogroups that contain at least one gene model from each of the compared Hordeum accessions. Shell orthogroups include gene models from at least two and at most 26Hordeum accessions. Gene models that were not assigned to any orthogroup (singletons) or were grouped only with genes from the same genotype were classified as cloud genes.

Open reading frames longer than 100 codons were searched for the presence of PPR and mTERF motifs using hmmsearch from the HMMER suite (http://hmmer.org) using hidden Markov models as defined in Cheng et al.86. for the PPR family and PF02536 from the Pfam 32.0 database (http://pfam.xfam.org)87 for the mTERF motif. Downstream processing of the hmmsearch results for the PPR proteins followed the pipeline described in Gutmann et al.88. The RfCTD domain recently identified as a unique feature of RFL-PPRs89 was included in the gene annotations. P-class and PLS-class genes with scores below 100 and 240, respectively, were excluded from the annotation as they are unlikely to represent functional PPR genes, as defined previously (IWGSC 2018)90.

The analyses described here used a number of tools from the toolkits vg (v1.61.0)91, odgi (v0.8.3-26-gbc7742ed)92, bcftools (v1.21)67 and seqkit (v2.9.0)72. All scripts used for graph construction and analysis are available at https://github.com/cropgeeks/panHordeum. Owing to computational limitations, we built an alignment of Hordeum whole genomes with Cactus47. We selected H. marinum BCC 2001 over H. marinum H559 on the basis of its higher assembly quality. Genome haplomes were soft-masked with bedtools69 using their respective repeat annotations. The guide tree required for the Cactus alignment was taken from the Orthofinder93 output generated as part of this study. Apart from setting appropriate resource parameters (that is, threads, memory and disk), we ran Cactus with default parameters. We transformed the resulting whole-genome alignment into a super-pangenome graph using hal2vg (https://github.com/ComparativeGenomicsToolkit/hal2vg), with the –noAncestors flag, and then further processed it with vg convert to get the final pangenome graph in GFA format (https://github.com/GFA-spec/GFA-spec). We computed basic graph statistics using odgi stats with the –summarize option, which included graph size, number of nodes, edges, paths and steps. To characterize the conservation of the different segments of the graph, we classified nodes as core, shell, or cloud. A node was considered ‘core’ if it was traversed by all samples’ paths, ‘cloud’ if it was traversed by a single sample’s path, and ‘shell’ otherwise. The same classification was done at the base level. Both computations were performed using the odgi toolkit (implementation details in class_stats.sh). To evaluate the agreement of haplotype sequences with their representation in the graph, we first extracted the linear sequences of all haplotypes as encoded in the graph using odgi paths with the –fasta option. These sequences were subsequently partitioned by source genome using seqkit grep, creating direct pairwise comparisons between input genomes and their graph-encoded counterparts. For each genome pair, we performed exact sequence matching, confirming whether each input sequence (or its reverse complement) was precisely preserved in the graph-encoded version (implementation details available in script fidelity.py). We computed pangenome graph growth curves based on the full graph using odgi heaps with 100 permutations of the input genomes. Results were plotted using script heaps_fit.R distributed with the odgi toolkit92. Whole-graph analysis turned out to be computationally prohibitive (job runtime limits and/or memory requirements) for several of the required tools from the vg and odgi toolkits, given a graph of this size and complexity. We therefore extracted subgraphs equating to individual chromosome paths for H. vulgare cv. Morex, which we used as the basis for all variant analyses. We used vg chunk for subgraph extraction. Variants were called from the chromosome-level subgraphs directly, using vg deconstruct. This generated VCF output containing the full range of variant sizes. To prepare structural variants from the graph for further analysis we broadly followed the variant decomposition approach used by the Human Pangenome Consortium94. This involved the removal of top-level variants of length >100,000 bp with vcfbub (https://github.com/pangenome/vcfbub), realigning alternate alleles against the reference for each variant using vcfwave (vcflib v1.0.2)95, and finally normalizing the resulting variants with bcftools norm67. We then added variant length information (SVLEN) to the VCF files with a custom script to allow extraction of structural variants based on the length difference between reference and alternate allele (>50 bp) and classified structural variations as deletions or insertions based on the directionality of the difference (insertion: string length REF  string length ALT). The resulting VCF files were converted to BED format with bcftools query. Variant density plots were computed with custom R scripts using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96. To explore the possibility of using the graph for read mapping and genotyping, we attempted to index the graph using vg gbwt/vg index/vg minimizer. This turned out to be computationally prohibitive in terms of job runtime limits on two separate compute facilities used, and thus we were unable to use the graph for the valuation of read mapping. We conducted graph-based conservation analysis with Pansel97, a tool used for calculation of diversity/conservation metrics directly from pan-genome graphs. The default bin size of 1kbp was used, along with all other parameters on default settings. Results were plotted using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96.

Single-copy genes were identified using BUSCO (v5.4.6)79 in B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)99, T. monococcum100, H. vulgare FT11 (ref. 19) and the 29 Hordeum haplomes collected in this study. Protein sequences of BUSCO single-copy genes present in all 34 haplomes were concatenated and aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101. Well-aligned regions were filtered using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was then constructed using RAxML (v8.2.12)103 with the PROTGAMMAWAG substitution model and the rapid bootstrap algorithm with 100 replicates. To facilitate genome-wide alignment, all 34 haplomes were masked using RepeatMasker (v4.1.1; http://www.repeatmasker.org) with a pan-genome TE library generated by panEDTA. The masked genomes and the inferred species tree were then used as input for Cactus (v2.6.5)47 to generate whole-genome MSAs. The loss rate of genomic elements was defined as the size of the reconstructed ancestral sequence at the corresponding genomic position in the multiple genome alignment.

To precisely construct phylogenetic trees and estimate divergence times within the genus Hordeum, we included four additional outgroup genomes: B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)104 (all downloaded from Ensembl Plants; https://plants.ensembl.org/index.html) and T. monococcum100 (https://wheat.pw.usda.gov/GG3/pangenome). We constructed phylogenetic trees using four approaches. The first two methods were based on whole-genome single-copy genes. Orthologous genes were identified from the genomes of our 34 Hordeum haplomes and four outgroup genomes using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82, yielding 2,198 single-copy genes. For the concatenation-based approach, the CDS sequences of these genes were concatenated and aligned with MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp, -b4 = 5, -b5=h; phylogenetic inference was then performed in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105. For the coalescence-based approach, the CDS sequences of each single-copy gene were aligned separately using MAFFT (v7.490)101, high-quality regions were selected with Gblocks (v0.91b)102 using the same parameters, individual gene trees were reconstructed with IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, and a species tree was inferred from these gene trees using ASTRAL-Pro3 (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)106. The remaining two methods were based on whole-genome MSAs generated with Cactus. In the CASTER-pair (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was used to infer a phylogenetic tree rooted with S. bicolor, while in the CASTER-site (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was analysed similarly but using site-based inference, also rooted with S. bicolor.

To estimate divergence times, genomic regions showing strong phylogenetic discordance (nRF > 0.21) were first excluded based on the genome-wide discordance analysis. 4DTV sites were extracted from MSAs of single-copy genes. Divergence times between barley and outgroup species were obtained from the TimeTree database (https://timetree.org/)108. Finally, species divergence times within the genus Hordeum were estimated using the MCMCtree program in PAML (v4.4)109.

We excluded multiple haplomes from the same species and retained a final set of 32 Hordeum haplomes for comparative analysis. All haplomes pairs were aligned against each other using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -2 -K 5 G -f 0.005 -x asm10, and the resulting alignments were stored in PAF format for visualization via dot plots. For each reference haplomes, we calculated the alignment coverage in non-overlapping 5 Mb windows, considering only alignments with a mapping quality greater than 20. Coverage values were normalized across the haplomes by the average coverage to produce normalized coverage profiles. In species that diverged more than 9 Ma, a bimodal distribution of normalized coverage was observed, allowing a threshold of 0.5 to distinguish distal and proximal regions (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Finally, genome-wide alignment and normalized coverage profiles were used to manually define the size and boundaries of proximal and distal regions across all species. Reverse-orientation alignments were extracted as indicators of putative inversion events. Two metrics were calculated for each pairwise comparison: (1) the number of reverse-orientation alignments per Mb and (2) the proportion of bases covered by reverse-orientation alignments. These metrics were separately calculated for proximal and distal chromosomal regions to compare the rates of inversion accumulation during species divergence. Linear regression models including divergence time, chromosomal region type (proximal or distal) and their interaction term were used to evaluate differences in the accumulation rates of reverse-orientation alignments between regions.

All other Hordeum genomes were aligned to the MorexV3 (ref. 28) reference genome using wfmash (v0.9.1-3; https://github.com/waveygang/wfmash) with the parameters -p 90 -l 0. Inversions were then identified using SyRI (v1.5.5)110 with parameters -F P -f–nosnp. Only inversions larger than 2 Mb and located outside of the proximal regions were retained for further analysis.

Based on the 2,198 single-copy orthologues identified in the section ‘Phylogeny and divergence time estimation’ and using the genome-wide concatenated single-copy gene tree as a reference, we conducted sliding-window gene tree analyses (Extended Data Fig. 6a). All single-copy genes were grouped into non-overlapping windows of 25 genes with a step size of 2 genes. Within each window, protein sequences were aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. Local window trees were built with FastTree (v2.1.11)111 (default GTR + CAT, 20 rate categories), starting from neighbour-joining trees and optimized with minimum-evolution and nearest-neighbour interchange moves; branch support was calculated using Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like values. Each resulting tree was rooted with S. bicolor as the outgroup using ETE3 (v3.1.2)112, and the nRF distance was calculated against the reference tree using the parameter –min_support_src 90. The nRF metric quantifies topological dissimilarity between trees, with values ranging from 0 (identical topology) to 1 (completely different topologies). Based on the nRF distribution, we identified 0.21 as a threshold to separate background from discordant signal peaks (Extended Data Fig. 6b). To evaluate the robustness of discordant region detection, we repeated the sliding-window analyses using alternative parameter settings (30 genes with step sizes of 1 and 5 genes). The major discordance peaks were consistently recovered across different window sizes and step lengths, indicating that peak detection was not sensitive to parameter selection (Supplementary Fig. 52). Genomic regions containing at least 10 overlap windows with nRF ≥ 0.21 were defined as candidate introgressed regions. For each candidate region, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the same procedure as for the genome-wide tree. The topological comparison of these local trees with the reference tree enabled the inference of introgression origins. The AU test113 implemented in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, was used to compare local reference trees and local phylogenetic trees. A P value (p-AU) lower than 0.05 indicated that the tree was significantly rejected.

Genomes of 20 diploid Hordeum species were searched for potential HGT genes from grasses of the subfamily Panicoideae. Regions of interest were identified in the genomes using BLAST (v2.12.0+)114 against four potential donor species: Panicum hallii (v3.2), Setaria italica (v2.2), Paspalum vaginatum (v3.1) and Paspalum notatum (GCA_036689595.1) (Supplementary Table 10). BLAST results were filtered to retain hits with a sequence identity of ≥95% and an alignment length of ≥150 bp. The same process was applied to H. vulgare cv. Morex (v3), which served as a negative control. H. vulgare is widely recognized as a species that lacks HGT genes from the Panicoideae subfamily39,41,42. Hits from potential donors that were found in both the Hordeum recipient genomes and H. vulgare were excluded from further analysis. This filtering was conducted using the intersect tool from BEDTools (v2.26.0)69, with an overlap threshold of 20%. Finally, the identified regions were compared with newly available annotations, and corresponding candidate genes were extracted. In this step, we identified 5,169 candidate genes.

To verify the foreign (that is, Panicoideae) origin of the candidate HGT genes identified as described above, phylogenetic trees were constructed for each candidate. Homologues were retrieved from a set of representative Poaceae species and two outgroups (Ananas comosus and Musa acuminata) (Supplementary Table 10) using BLASTn (e-value cutoff of 10−10). The retrieved sequences were aligned with the Hordeum HGT gene candidates using MUSCLE (v3.8)115. The alignments were trimmed using trimAl (v1.2) with an automated trimming method116. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using PhyML (v3.1)117, with 1,000 bootstrap iterations and the GTR substitution model. The resulting trees were reviewed semi-automatically with the assistance of the Newick Utilities suite118. A candidate gene was considered a true HGT gene if the gene sequence was nested within the PACMAD clade. TE-related genes were filtered out and only high-confidence, protein-coding genes were retained for further analysis. Out of 5,169 candidate genes, 4,393 did not pass through the primary phylogenetic validation and 776 genes remained. Candidate genes that passed the first step of verification were cross-referenced with orthogroups previously created during pan-genome construction. For groups containing more than one candidate gene, a consensus sequence was generated using MAFFT (v7.520)102 for MSA, followed by the cons tool from EMBOSS (v6.5.7.0)119 to produce the consensus. These consensus sequences were subsequently used for BLASTn searches. Hits from at least five species, including minimally one from Panicoideae, were required for tree construction. Phylogenetic trees were then constructed as described above, using MAFFT as the aligner. Alignments and trees were reviewed manually: orthogroups supporting the HGT scenario were retained, and genes in these groups were classified as either foreign or native, based on their position on the tree. The neighbour of transferred genes was marked as presumed donor if the branch represented one genus or species, otherwise the donor was marked as unknown. The entire orthogroup was considered to have a native copy if it contained at least one gene marked ‘native’, regardless of which species that gene was present in.

To determine the transfer times of genes during the evolutionary history of the lineage, an ancestral state reconstruction was conducted for each gene independently. The marginal ancestral state was inferred using the equal rate model120, applying the maximum-likelihood approach described by Pagel121 and implemented in the phytools package122. To ensure accuracy, the results were verified and adjusted for cases where genes were found in multiple tips but not in their common ancestor. In such instances, the presence of the gene was manually introduced at the ancestor node. For each node in the phylogenetic tree, both the originally reconstructed values and the manually adjusted values were visualized.

Genes from all orthogroups were annotated using eggNOG-mapper web server (v2.1.12)123,124. Gene Ontology terms were extracted for each group and enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package (v4.14.3), with a significance threshold of an adjusted P value of 0.05 (ref. 125).

RNA-seq data for inflorescence, leaf and root tissues previously generated for 19 Hordeum species were used in this study (RNA-seq data for H. bulbosum were not available). Read trimming on quality (Q30) and removal of sequencing adapters were done using Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Cleaned reads from each library were then mapped to the corresponding reference genome using the STAR aligner (v2.7.7a)127. Quantification of mapped reads was done using the subread package v1.5.2 with featureCounts (v2.0.1)128 followed by normalization using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method implemented in the edgeR package (v4.2.1)129. Genes were considered to be expressed if TMM ≥ 1 in at least one tissue.

Structurally intact and fragmented TEs were annotated for each genome using the panEDTA (v0.1) pipeline31. In addition to the curated TREP database (https://trep-db.uzh.ch/)130, TE classification followed the EDTA ontology (https://github.com/oushujun/EDTA/blob/master/bin/TE_Sequence_Ontology.txt), with manual curation of TE categories. High-confidence gene models from H. vulgare cv. MorexV3 was supplied via the -cds parameter to exclude genic sequences from TE annotation. For each genome, the length, classification, insertion time and divergence metrics of intact LTR retrotransposons were extracted from the intact.gff3 and pass.list output files. To investigate TE family expansion and intergenomic relationships, we used the TEpop framework (https://github.com/wicker314/TEpop) to treat each TE as an individual sample for population structure analysis46. PCA was then performed using FlashPCA2 (ref. 131) to explore the major patterns of TE variation across Hordeum species. To infer the formation time of tetraploid genomes from TE bursts, full-length LTR/Copia elements were extracted from tetraploid assemblies and clustered using CD-HIT (v4.8.1)132 with the parameters -n 5 -c 0.9 -d 0 -aL 0.9 -aS 0.9 -g 1 based on sequence similarity. To avoid potential bias caused by large-scale segmental exchanges between subgenomes, genomic regions identified as exchanged segments were excluded from this analysis (Supplementary Table 13). TEs that were shared between polyploid subgenomes but absent from their corresponding diploid progenitors were defined as post-allopolyploidization insertions. The insertion time distributions of these elements were used to reconstruct TE dynamics after subgenome fusion, and the onset of the insertion peak was used to estimate the timing of polyploid genome formation.

To identify conserved elements across Hordeum genomes, outgroup species were removed from the HAL alignment file using halRemoveGenome in Cactus (v2.6.5). Genome-wide MSAs were then extracted in MAF format using cactus-hal2maf with the parameters “–chunkSize 1000000–noAncestors–onlyOrthologs–noDupes”, using MorexV3 as the reference genome. Alignment blocks containing fewer than 10 sequences were filtered out in MSAs. A neutral model of evolution was fitted to the Hordeum phylogeny using fourfold degenerate sites from chromosome 3H of barley, using phyloFit from the PHAST package (v1.4)133. Based on the genome-wide multiple alignments and the trained neutral model, conserved elements were identified using PhastCons with the “–most-conserved” flag. The conserved and non-conserved models were trained with a target genome coverage of 0.45, and the expected length of conserved elements was set to 8 bp.

ATAC–seq libraries were prepared from fresh leaf tissue at 3–5 leaf stage. Nuclei were isolated by fine chopping the tissue in isolation buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, 1% Trion X-100, 5 mM β-Mercaptoethanol) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Following isolation, nuclei were quantified via flow cytometry and 75,000 nuclei were subjected to tagmentation using the Tagment DNA Enzyme (TDE1, Illumina) at 37 °C for 30 min. Transposed DNA was purified using the MinElute PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen), libraries were amplified with NEBNext High-Fidelity 2x PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs), and the final library purification was performed using VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (Vazyme) according to standard protocols from the manufacturers. Libraries were quantified as described previously62 and sequenced (paired-end, 2× 151 cycles, Illumina NovaSeq 6000, IPK Gatersleben) following protocols provided by the manufacturer (Illumina).

Adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed using Trim Galore (v0.6.4_dev; https://github.com/FelixKrueger/TrimGalore.git) with the following parameters: -q 25–phred33–stringency 3–length 60–paired -j 10. Only read pairs with both ends retained were used in subsequent analyses. Trimmed reads were aligned to the reference genome using BWA (v0.7.17)134. The resulting SAM files were converted to BAM format and sorted using SAMtools (v1.10)67. Only properly paired reads with mapping quality ≥ 30 were retained (-f 2 -F 1804 -q 30), and further sorted by read name to enable mate information correction using samtools fixmate. Duplicate reads were marked using Picard MarkDuplicates (v2.21.9, https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) with VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=LENIENT and REMOVE_DUPLICATES=false. After marking, only properly paired, non-duplicate reads were retained and re-sorted by coordinate to produce final cleaned BAM files for downstream analysis. BAM indices were generated using samtools index. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1)135. The effective genome size (-g) was set to 4.2 Gb, approximating the size of the barley genome. Peaks were called with automatic threshold evaluation (–cutoff-analysis), and all duplicate reads were retained during the analysis to preserve biological signal.

VRN1 and ZCCT genes were identified in all assembled wild barley genomes using blastn searches (blast-plus/2.12.0)114 with VRN1 MorexV3 (NC_058522.1:c528157887–528147799) and NCBI GenBank ZCCTa/b/c queries (AY485977, AY485978 and AY687931). Corresponding regions were extracted from genome assemblies by bedtools (v2.26.0)69 and manually annotated and analysed by Geneious Prime software (v2024.0.5; https://www.geneious.com). Sequence similarity visualization of the 2 kb region upstream of the transcription start site and the first intron of VRN1 genes was done by flexidot (v1.06)136. The 79-bp deletion in H. cordobense and H. muticum VRN1 gene was detected by MSA of the extracted VRN1 sequences from wild Hordeum species and winter cultivar Igri in Geneious Prime software (v2023.0.4; https://www.geneious.com) with MAFFT101. The critical region of cultivar Igri was identified in a previous study51.

Three biological replicates were analysed for each stage (14 DAG, 28 DAG) of H. cordobense and H. californicum grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod). Total RNA was extracted from frozen leaf tissue using a Quick-RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research). RNA quality and concentration were evaluated with a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies) on RNA 6000 Nano chips (Agilent Technologies). H. cordobense 28 DAG RNA-seq libraries and small RNA-seq libraries were constructed according to Illumina instructions and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 platform at Novogene. Other sequencing libraries (H. cordobense 14 DAG and H. californicum 14 and 28 DAG; small RNA and RNA-seq) were constructed at the Institute of Experimental Botany (Olomouc) using NEBNext Multiplex Small RNA Library Prep Set for Illumina and NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina with poly-A selection and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, 150 PE mode.

Small RNA-seq read trimming and sequencing adaptor removal were done with cutadapt (v3.4)137. Only reads of length 21–24 nt were used for subsequent analyses. ShortStack (v4)138 was used to map small RNA reads to the corresponding genome with default parameters. Bigwig files were created from bam files in a combination of samtools (v1.11)67 and deepTools (v3.5.6)139 with parameters bigwigAverage, bamCoverage–binSize 10,–normalizeUsing BPM. Visualization of small RNA and mRNA bigwig files were done with pyGenomeTracks (v3.9)140.

RNA-seq read trimming on quality (Q30) and sequencing adaptor removal were done with Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Resulting high-quality reads from each library were mapped onto the corresponding reference genome using STAR (v2.7.7a)127, with default parameters. Mapped reads quantification was done by rsem (v1.3.3)141.

Ten seeds per each of 14 selected Hordeum species accessions (BCC 2067 H. cordobense, BCC 2058 H. californicum, BCC 2014 H. muticum, BCC 2055 H. jubatum, BCC 2001 H. marinum, BCC 2009 H. murinum subsp. murinum, BCC 2017 H. murinum subsp. glaucum, BCC 2023 H. flexuosum, BCC 2026 H. erectifolium, BCC 2028 H. pubiflorum, BCC 2043 H. pusillum, BCC 2059 H. intercedens, BCC 2065 H. patagonicum and BCC 2069 H. roshevitzii) were used. Spring cultivated barley genotypes Morex and Golden Promise and winter genotypes Igri and Antonella were included as controls and were treated identically to wild species. Seeds were stratified at 4 °C for 4 days, germinated in Petri dishes on moist filter paper and then transferred to soil. Plants were grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod) in a growth chamber and cultivated until senescence. Days to flowering were scored in three-day intervals, and the plants were considered flowering at the first emergence of the awn tips. Plants were imaged using a Nikon D5600 digital camera.

The elongated outer glume 1 (eog1) mutants from cultivated barley59, including eog1.a (GSHO 1891), eog1.c (GSHO 1892), eog1.e (GSHO 285) and macrolepis (lep-e.1; GSHO 960), were obtained from the Barley Genetic Stock Collection. Several mutants, namely M2342, M9630, M9815 and M11405, were identified from independent M2 lines of the previously established barley HTX mutagenesis population142. SEM observations were conducted using a Hitachi SEM SU8081 following a standard protocol143. Young inflorescences were sampled and examined. Allelism test was performed by crossing M9630 with GSHO 1891 and GSHO 1892, respectively. All F1 progeny exhibited elongated glumes on the central fertile spikelet (Extended Data Fig. 12d). Sequence-specific amplification of the C2H2-zinc-finger transcription factor gene was performed using primers T-70820-F (5′-TAGGACCGCATATTTCCAGG-3′) and T-70820-R (5′-GAACAGTTCCAAGGCGAAAG-3′). The resulting amplicons were sequenced using Sanger sequencing.

Clean reads (Supplementary Table 20) were obtained by removing the adapters, reads containing N bases and low-quality reads using fastp (v0.20.1) with default parameters144. Clean reads were mapped to their respective reference genomes via Hisat2 v2.1.0 with default parameters145. Read counts were determined from the mapping files via featureCounts (v2.0.1) using standard parameters128, and the TPM values of each gene were calculated. Spike-specific expressed genes were defined as having less than 5% TPM in other tissues146. The heatmap was generated using the pheatmap R package (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pheatmap) based on the normalized TPM values. Venn diagrams were drawn using the eulerr package (v6.1.0; https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eulerr). A local BLAST search was performed using the deduced amino acids of HORVU.MOREX.r3.2HG0170820.1 (EOG1) as the query against the 24 Hordeum genome sequences to identify homologous proteins. Amino acid sequence alignment was carried out using MUSCLE (v3.8)115, and the resulting MSA was visualized with the Simple MSA Viewer function of TBtools II147.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All sequence data generated in this study have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) under umbrella BioProject PRJEB128330. Accession codes for individual accessions are listed in Supplementary Table 3 (genome sequencing) and Supplementary Table 6 (transcriptome sequencing). The assemblies and annotations are available for download from the IPK Galaxy server (https://galaxy-web.ipk-gatersleben.de/libraries). Gene and TE annotations, MSAs and coordinates of conserved regions have been deposited at the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2026/11). The pangenome graph in GFA format has been deposited in the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2025/12).

Code for gene annotation, pangenomic analyses and graph construction is available at GitHub (https://github.com/PGSB-HMGU/BPGv2, https://github.com/jia-wu-feng/Pan_Hordeum and https://github.com/cropgeeks/panHordeum).

(a) Representative images showing whole plant architecture and spike morphology for 20 species in the genus Hordeum. Species shown (left to right, top to bottom): H. erectifolium, H. stenostachys, H. pusillum, H. euclaston, H. intercedens, H. patagonicum, H. pubiflorum, H. flexuosum, H. chilense, H. muticum, H. cordobense, H. californicum, H. jubatum, H. roshevitzii, H. secalinum, H. bogdanii, H. gussoneanum, H. marinum, H. bulbosum, and H. murinum subsp. glaucum. Each panel displays a whole plant (left) and a close-up of the spike (right), highlighting variation in growth habit and inflorescence morphology across the genus. Note that the scale bars differ: the scale bar for whole plant images represents 16 cm, while the scale bar for spike images represents 1 cm. Images show representative plants of the indicated species/accessions; no independent experimental replication was performed for this descriptive panel. (b) Pie-chart providing ratios of conserved- and variable- genes for all Hordeum pangenome accessions. Bar chart illustrating the number of genes shared between different combinations of accessions within the Hordeum pangenome. Genes shared by all 27 accessions constitute the core genome while genes private to a single species are referred to as the cloud genome. (c) Bar chart illustrating the proportion of genes contained in the core-, shell-, and cloud- gene portions by individual accessions.

(a) NLR gene copy numbers across 34 Hordeum haplomes. The central line in each boxplot represents the median; the box spans the interquartile range (IQR), and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. TNL: Contain TIR, NBS, and LRR domains. CNL: Contain CC, NBS, and LRR domains. RNL: Contain RPW8, NBS, and LRR domains. RN: Contain RPW8 and NBS domains only. NL: Contain NBS and LRR domains, but lack TIR, CC, and RPW8. TN: Contain TIR and NBS domains only. CN: Contain CC and NBS domains only. NBS-only: Contain only the NBS domain. TIR = Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor-like; NBS = Nucleotide-Binding Site; LRR = Leucine-Rich Repeat; CC = Coiled-Coil; RPW8 = Resistance to Powdery Mildew 8-like domain. (b) Comparison of NLR copy numbers among Hordeum genomes. Welch’s t-test revealed a highly significant difference between the I genome group and other genome groups (two-sided Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6). (c) Bar chart showing the number of accessions represented in each NLR orthogroup (OG). The x-axis indicates accession count per OG. The pie chart summarizes conserved vs. variable genes across 27 accessions. (d) Distribution of NLR gene clusters (≥3 genes) across 34 haplomes. Dot size represents the number of genes per cluster. The chr4H/chr5H group showed significantly different values compared to other chromosomes (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P < 2.2 × 10−16).

(a) Complete set of chromosome 4H dotplot comparisons between Hordeum genomes spanning different divergence times, complementing the representative comparisons shown in Fig. 1c. Two species were randomly selected from each phylogenetic node for sequence alignment (Supplementary Table 11). Numbers above the dotplots indicate the estimated divergence times (Ma) between the species shown on the x- and y-axes. (b) Normalized coverage density plot in H. euclaston. The right shows species ordered by divergence time (Ma); two distinct peaks appear among species that diverged over 9 million years ago. (c) Comparison of chromosome 4H between H. vulgare and H. euclaston. The bar plots along the x- and y-axes represent normalized coverage in 5 Mb windows. Coverage was calculated based on whole-genome alignment between H. vulgare and H. euclaston. Proximal and distal regions were defined using a normalized coverage threshold of 0.5.

(a) Proportion of repeat types in proximal and distal regions. (b) Boxplot showing the difference in repeat composition between distal and proximal regions. LTR/Gypsy, LTR/unknown and low_complexity showed significant proximal enrichment (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10, P = 1.86 × 10−9 and P = 9.31 × 10−10, respectively). For the box plots, the center line represents the median, the box bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, and the whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range (IQR) from the box boundaries; points beyond the whiskers are shown as outliers. (c) A schematic diagram of the “stretch-and-twist” model. (d) Genome-wide distribution of distal inversions (≥2 Mb) across Hordeum haplomes.

Dotplot comparisons of the chr1A: 400–650 Mb region between T. monococcum and the remaining genomes, complementing the representative comparisons shown in Fig. 2a. Colors indicate different clusters and are consistent with those used in Fig. 2a.

(a) Schematic overview of the hybridization scanning method. (b) Density distribution of normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distances. The red line (nRF = 0.21) represents the empirical threshold separating the two peaks corresponding to background phylogenetic variation and regions with elevated phylogenetic discordance. (c) Distribution of normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distances between local gene trees and the species-wide reference tree across the genome. The phylogenetic tree was reconstructed using concatenated single-copy genes located within this region, with bootstrap values shown at each node. Red branches indicate topological changes relative to the genome-wide reference species tree. The local phylogeny revealed segmental exchanges between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum BCC2005 and between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. jubatum. An Approximately Unbiased (AU) test supported the local phylogenetic topology (p-AU = 1.0) and rejected the genome-wide reference topology (p-AU = 2.11 × 10−84). An AU test supported the local phylogenetic topology (p-AU = 1.0) and rejected the genome-wide reference topology (p-AU = 6.55 × 10−57).

Chelsea are reportedly stepping up their efforts to sign Real Betis wonderkid Jose Antonio Morante, with Manchester United and Manchester City also interested in securing the highly-rated winger’s signature.

The 19-year-old has emerged as one of Spain’s most exciting young prospects after impressive performances at youth international level and a breakthrough into senior football.

According to a report from TEAMtalk, Chelsea’s ownership group BlueCo have already made an approach to Real Betis in an attempt to sign the talented attacker. However, their initial efforts were unsuccessful, with the Spanish club determined to retain his services.

Chelsea first identified Morante during the European Under-19 Championship in Wales, where he produced an outstanding campaign and finished as the competition’s leading goalscorer, helping Spain lift the trophy.

His performances clearly caught the attention of the Blues’ recruitment department, who have continued monitoring his development since the tournament.

Morante has also made an encouraging start to senior football, scoring on his first-team debut for Betis in a convincing 5-2 win over Osasuna last month.

Chelsea are not the only Premier League side keeping a close eye on the teenager, with Manchester United and Manchester City also holding discussions about a potential move.

Both clubs have been impressed by his rapid development and believe he could become an important attacking prospect in the coming years. His performances for Spain’s youth sides have further strengthened his reputation among some of Europe’s leading recruitment departments.

However, competition for his signature is not limited to English football. Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund are also monitoring his situation, while Atletico Madrid have expressed interest in the talented youngster.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Real Betis will be desperate to avoid losing another promising academy graduate, particularly after witnessing his impressive progress over recent months. The Spanish outfit handed him a new long-term contract during the summer to protect his future.

Nevertheless, growing interest from several European heavyweights could make it increasingly difficult for Betis to hold on to their prized asset.

Chelsea have already demonstrated their determination by making an initial approach, and it remains to be seen whether they return with an improved proposal in the coming months.

Morante’s attacking qualities and potential make him an attractive long-term investment, although the Blues will face considerable competition if they decide to intensify their pursuit.

#1340. Inter eye deal for Lazio defender following Stones struggles

La Gazzetta dello Sport reports that John Stones’ fitness issues have sparked Inter’s interest in Lazio defender Oliver Provstgaard for next summer.

Inter have set their sights on 23-year-old Lazio defender Provstgaard, according to Gazzetta.

The report claims the defending Serie A champions are already planning to add a new centre-back for next season, also due to Stones’ physical issues.

Lazio’s asking price for the Denmark international is close to €40m, a fee the Nerazzurri will only be able to afford at the end of the season, not in the January window.

According to Gazzetta, Davide Frattesi’s move to Lazio over the summer might even help the Nerazzurri to lower Lazio’s demands.

Frattesi joined Lazio in a €5m loan deal last summer, and the Biancocelesti hold an option to buy for a further €10m.

Inter have a 50% sell-on clause, and re-discussing the terms of the agreement might help them get a better deal for Provstgaard in the summer.

Inter saw Stefan de Vrij, Matteo Darmian and Francesco Acerbi leave the club at the end of their contracts in June 2026, replacing them by signing Stones as a free agent from Manchester City and retaining Benjamin Pavard after his return from a one-season loan spell at Marseille.

Stones has struggled with injuries this season and has just returned to training after nearly two months out. The England international suffered a muscle strain in the flexor muscles of his left thigh in mid-September and was an unused substitute in Inter’s latest Serie A match against Como, just before the break.

The England international has made four appearances across all competitions this season, and his contract at the Stadio Meazza expires in June 2028.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1339. Why Juventus have not called Conte as Carnevali’s main candidate named

Tuttosport reports that Juventus continue to have confidence in Luciano Spalletti and are not considering replacing their coach mid-season, but if they were to make a change in 2027-28, Giovanni Carnevali would prefer Simone Inzaghi over Antonio Conte.

Former Juventus midfielder and coach Conte has strongly confirmed his desire to return to the Allianz Stadium one day, predicting that “sooner or later the circle will close.”

Conte already coached Juventus from 2011 to 2014, winning the first three Serie A titles in the post-Calciopoli era. This is not the first time the Italian tactician has openly admitted his desire to return to the club one day, but that doesn’t mean it will happen.

Tuttosport insists Juventus are not considering replacing their coach, Spalletti, this season. First, the Serie A giants still trust the Tuscan tactician; second, they are reluctant to make another managerial change that would bring in their fourth coach in four years.

Club owners and directors are convinced that even appointing Conte midseason would not address the team’s lack of personality or the players’ lack of responsibility, especially with frequent changes on the bench in the coming years.

Spalletti remains under contract until 2028, and the club will assess his results at the end of the season.

If, however, the Bianconeri change coach in 2027-28, Conte might not be their top candidate, Tuttosport claims.

Carnevali, in fact, seems to favour a different option, such as ex-Inter coach Simone Inzaghi. The Piacenza-born tactician might not be every Juventus fan’s cup of tea because of his past with the Nerazzurri, but even Conte’s potential appointment isn’t widely approved, given how he left the club one day into the 2014-15 pre-season and his move to Inter a few years later.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1338. Report Milan dream of signing McTominay thanks to new kit deal

Milan’s new lucrative kit deal with Adidas will allow the Rossoneri to make a big-money signing, and according to QN, one of their top target is Napoli’s Scott McTominay.

Napoli star McTominay has reportedly attracted Milan’s interest. Italian newspaper Quotidiano Nazionale notes that the Rossoneri are keeping a close eye on the Scottish international, especially after agreeing to a new kit deal with Adidas.

Their agreement, which will begin in 2028, will last ten years and bring €50m per season to the Serie A giants.

This future financial boost isn’t the only reason Adidas might help Milan sign the Napoli star, who is one of the German company’s testimonials.

Furthermore, McTominay’s contract with Napoli expires in June 2028, and the two parties have yet to reach an agreement despite ongoing negotiations.

QN confirms that McTominay has requested a new €7m-a-year contract to extend his stay at the Stadio Maradona.

TMW reported the same fee just a few days ago, saying the midfielder’s demands are unlikely to be matched by any Serie A club.

Yet, this latest report suggests that Milan’s new agreement with Adidas might put the Rossoneri in a privileged position in the race for the Scottish star.

#1337. Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, said.

“We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”

The Welshman controls it exquisitely with a bit of footwork before being hauled to ground. Tigers are brought back for a pen, and Searle puts boot to ball in front of the posts. You feel Tigers have a bit of daylight now between their rivals.

That scrum before the Cameron Henderson try feels like a significant moment. There’s nothing a Welford Road full house likes to see more than an opposition pack on rollerskates at the set piece and that was Northampton in full retreat.

You could sense the psychological lift it gave Leicester and, on the back of the lineout drive try that kicked off the second half from Jamie Blamire, it feels like a hard road back for Northampton.

They’re not the champions for nothing, though.

The momentum is with Leicester now. The hosts come forward again and Searle tries to find Radwan out wide with a toe-poke but Steward is there to carry it into touch. Leicester aren’t done just yet - Blamire chucks in another clean arrow - and the forwards to do the rest.

Everybody on Saints’ tryline is expecting Heyes to pick-and-go but the prop catches them all by surprise by astutely popping it up to Carnduff, who bundles over.

It’s hasn’t been a good day from the tee for Searle, who misses another.

Play resumes and it’s a same Saints’ scrum, but Tigers get a huge shove on - Joe Heyes is in the thick of it - and the Tigers’ pack roar. The crowd loved that one.

The hosts kick to the corner, Blamire’s arrow is safely gathered by Henderson and the Tigers execute a superb training park move. Kata wins the collision and Heyes is among a number of decoy runners as JVP recycles quickly and the hosts spread it wide to Hamer-Webb, who finds Henderson on his outside. We have rugby again! Tigers go to the skies from the restart - Hamer-Webb gives chase - but doesn’t roll away and Saints wrestle back momentum, but can’t seem to sustain it and the hosts win it back. Steward does well to avoid being ambushed into touch - there’s a different intensity to the hosts this half, but neither side are having much luck keeping possession.

Pollock continues to give the hosts a headache, ripping the ball and Saints have the put-in at the scrum. The visitors ship it away quickly but play is stopped as Blamire, down injured, is attended to.

A 10-point match so far in rainy conditions - not much to write home about other than the confrontation before the break. Tigers begin on the front foot and win an offside penalty and for what seems like the umpteenth time in this match kick to the corner. Have they tidied up their lineout? They’ve kept this one as simple as possible with a short throw-in.

Kundiona is pernalised for a high tackle on JVP. Another penalty Tigers.. and this time they make it count! Throw, catch, drive and they’re over as Blamire finds his way to the line. It’s route one stuff. Searle can’t add the conversion.

Well, that was lively anyway. Full-scale conflagration to end a largely unwatchable half.

It was triggered by Alex Mitchell, of all people laughing, at Adam Radwan after he had been carried into touch in the final play of the half by George Hendy and Henry Pollock. Radwan took exception and from there things accelerated.

Leicester captain Ollie Chessum was at the heart of the pushing and shoving, snapping at Pollock in an argument that carried on with some pushing and shoving in the tunnel.

It gave the crowd something to get excited about after a poor 40 minutes.

Sometimes you get good games in bad conditions but this isn’t one of them.

Northampton have had the better of things but just when they look capable of getting their intricate interplay going there is a handling error.

Leicester’s defence, roared on with ‘Tigers, Tigers’ chants whenever the home side are on the back foot can take some credit for that.

They are still very much in this, four points adrift, but the tightness of the scoreline is the best that can be said for this contest so far.

Leicester were buoyed in the week by re-signing Jack van Poortfliet, who extended his contract with his boyhood club.

I grew up supporting Leicester, it’s always been my club,” said the England scrum half. This place feels like home in my rugby life. The club is in a really good position, I think we have a great group of lads and great coaches.

I love playing rugby here, I have my best mates here and I believe that we’ve got a group of lads that we can do great things with. I want to be in a place that I love playing for and I believe can win trophies.”

Squally conditions this afternoon at Mattioli Welford Road - in fact make that horrible. An interesting test then for Northampton as lovers of the beautiful game.

You would imagine that the rain and wind would suit a Leicester side whose DNA is set piece power better.

Expect the catch and drive to get plenty of game time and Jack van Poortvliet and Billy Searle to go to the air regularly. It could be a stern examination for teenage Saints full-back James Pater.

It’s a big day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Northampton Saints: J Pater; T Freeman, R Hutchinson, F Dingwall, G Hendy; F Smith, A Mitchell, E Iyogun, C Langdon, C Kundiona, A Coles, E Prowse, J Kemeny, T Pearson, H Pollock.

Replacements: R Smith, D Fischetti, I Neculai, JJ Van Der Mescht, T Lockett, C Chick, A McParland, O Sleightholme.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.
